title: 5 unmissable artworks you can see for free at Frieze Sculpture 2026
author: India Lawrence
content:
[title]
Every autumn, the Frieze art fair takes over Regent’s Park in central London, bringing with it the crème de la crème of the art world. But with tickets to the fair costing upwards of £100, its punters are mostly the all-black-wearing, unusual-haircut-sporting industry elites who can actually afford the pieces on offer.
But that’s why Frieze Sculpture is so great. The annual exhibition is staged in the open air of Regent’s Park and is totally free to visit, meaning us regular folk can still get a slice of the arty pie.
Curated by London-based curator and writer Fatoş Üstek, this year the display is designed as a web of interconnected objects, linked together by materials, stories and communities, under the loose theme of ‘hybridity’. We went along to have a look. Here are the five best sculptures we saw.
The 5 best sculptures at Frieze London 2026
![A blue door opening into the ground with steps leading below the earth](https://media.timeout.com/images/106448683/image.webp) 
1. ‘Dreams and Salt’, Angel Otero
There’s something of both The Truman Show and Monsters Inc to this intriguing azure door poking up out of the ground. Behind the open door, steps – either an entrance or an exit, depending on your interpretation – lead into a dark void beneath the earth. According to Otero, the sculpture is emblematic of migration, representing the emotional distance that grows between a person and their homeland.
![Blue bronze sculpture of a warrior figure on a colourful plinth](https://media.timeout.com/images/106448685/image.webp) 
2. ‘Warrior Figure’, Ramesh Mario Nithiyendran
Quite the jaunty little fellow, Ramesh Mario Nithiyendran’s two-metre-tall figure has golden shells for its nipples, clay pots rising from its shoulders and appears to have a septum piercing. Drawing on South Asian artistic tradition, Warrior Figure has two faces. It was built in wet clay and cast in bronze using an ancient wax technique.
![Elliptical sculpture made of perforated anodised aluminium in Regent's Park](https://media.timeout.com/images/106448679/image.webp) 
3. ‘Eye of the Needle’, Conrad Shawcross
This is an artwork you could stare at for hours. Conrad Shawcross’s mesmerising elliptical monolith is made from perforated anodised aluminium. Inspired by the concept of deep time and cosmic geometry, looking through this piece’s awesome hexagonal tessellations feels like being hypnotised.
![Black palm tree sculpture made from tryes and steel](https://media.timeout.com/images/106448676/image.webp) 
4. ‘Black Palm’, Douglas White
This towering seven-metre-tall palm tree is intimidating in its stature. Crafted from reclaimed steel and tyres sourced from roadsides in Central America, it’s hard not to think of forest fires when looking at its blackened exterior and ragged tyre-palm leaves.
![Wormlike sculpture made of discarded materials in Regent's Park](https://media.timeout.com/images/106448682/image.webp) 
5. ‘Wyrm’, Catriona Robertson
Appearing like a giant worm bursting from the soil, Catriona Robertson’s sculpture is crafted from reclaimed plywood, timber and corrugated iron and has a childlike playfulness to it. By using discarded urban materials, Robertson’s work directly references the changing city landscape.
These are the 10 London art exhibitions we’re most excited about in autumn 2026.
Get the latest and greatest from the Big Smoke – from news and reviews to events and trends. Just follow our Time Out London WhatsApp channel.
Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox
summary: Frieze Sculpture is a free, annual open-air exhibition held in Regent's Park in central London, offering an accessible alternative to the main Frieze art fair. Curated by Fatoş Üstek around the theme of "hybridity," this year's display features interconnected objects linked by materials, stories, and communities. The exhibition showcases notable works by international artists, including Angel Otero, Ramesh Mario Nithiyendran, Conrad Shawcross, Douglas White, and Catriona Robertson.
key_points: Frieze Sculpture in Regent's Park is totally free to visit, unlike the main Frieze art fair which requires expensive tickets.
The 2026 exhibition is curated by Fatoş Üstek under the loose theme of "hybridity."
Angel Otero's 'Dreams and Salt' features an azure door leading into a dark void, representing migration and emotional distance.
Ramesh Mario Nithiyendran's 'Warrior Figure' is a two-metre-tall bronze sculpture drawing on South Asian artistic traditions.
Douglas White's seven-metre-tall 'Black Palm' is constructed from reclaimed steel and tyres.

title: Is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?
author: Annabel Rackham
content:
![Models backstage ahead of the M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026 at The Design Museum on September 18, 2026 in London, England.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/016f/live/14feaea0-b365-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026
- Published
"I'm the first person to be like, 'It's from M&S, you need to get on to it,'" Farron Clark, a 26-year-old brand strategist tells me. She says it's officially cool to buy your clothes from the high street retailer now.
According to Clark and others on social media, Marks and Spencer is becoming the hot place to shop for women under 35, while also keeping its core older audience happy too.
"For a long time M&S had this fusty reputation - it was less valued by younger people," says Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial content at British Vogue, who tells the BBC there is now a "fresh energy around the brand".
And accompanying that fresh energy is a new marketing strategy, which includes hosting its first-ever London Fashion Week show on Friday, featuring a collection of outfits inspired by the brand's archive.
So how is M&S attracting and retaining a younger generation of shoppers in a highly competitive market? The BBC went to the catwalk show and spoke to experts to find out.
![A composite image of various models wearing M&S garments on the catwalk at London Fashion Week](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1056/cpsprodpb/64c7/live/c167ba40-b367-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.png)
Speaking ahead of the event at the Design Museum, the company's head of womenswear design, Lisa Illis, says they wanted to do this because of the "immediacy of seeing something and being able to own it and wear it, rather than waiting six months".
For many, M&S is more synonymous with pig-shaped sweets than cutting-edge fashion, but its runway of 43 womenswear and 10 menswear looks did a lot to persuade people that the latter is where its true talent lie.
Normally Fashion Week is about seeing what you'll be wearing six months from now, but this runway was full of colder weather fits, from opulent faux fur jackets and wrist cuffs, to satin jumpsuits and dresses in rich tones of navy, burgundy and brown.
The catwalk featured a diverse range of models in age, size and gender, demonstrating the brand's desire to cater to a wide market.
But there was certainly a concerted effort to attract the eye of younger shoppers with a fashion-forward approach to Christmas party staples like sequinned dresses, tasselled skirts and see-through lace tops.
'They have created a modern version of everything we know and love'
![Womenswear and menswear collections](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/dd54/live/5a857d60-b341-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
Womenswear and menswear collections at London Fashion Week are inspired by the M&S archive
The retailer has been focusing on "newer styles and relevant trends" to attract younger customers, says Illis.
But she says that this has been achieved without compromising on quality which is what keeps M&S's core audience on board.
"They have created a modern version of everything we know and love - cashmere staples, knitwear and the lingerie department," says Nnadi.
Clark agrees that M&S has been nailing "funnel neck [styles] and barrel jeans, which are filtering down from high fashion".
M&S has perhaps been fortunate to rebrand at a time when consumer habits are changing, as young shoppers consider buying capsule wardrobes - a smaller number of staple pieces that can be styled in a variety of ways.
Clark notes that the idea of wear-it-once fast fashion has declined as people "are looking for [foundational pieces] to rotate".
This is something Perrie Sian, one of Britain's biggest fashion influencers, has also noticed. The 34-year-old tells the BBC: "The real height of fast fashion is behind us".
"As a group we've changed our shopping habits and M&S slots into that," she says. "In my content and with lots of other creators we're showing people how to wear things in multiple ways, how to look after them."
She added that she is noticing "people are willing to spend a little bit more" on wardrobe staples and items that "wash well and are made of cotton, not acrylic or polyester".
![A composite image of various models wearing M&S garments on the catwalk at London Fashion Week](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1056/cpsprodpb/55f7/live/58212af0-b36a-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.png)
'Having a walk around M&S with my friends is the perfect Saturday'
During the Covid pandemic M&S struggled, but returned to growth in 2022-2023, with its fashion, home and beauty market share reaching 9.6%.
This again increased in 2023-2024 to 10%, and 10.5% in 2024-2025.
But the business took a big hit in 2025 due to a cyber attack, which left shoppers unable to use its website and app and affected stock in stores too.
It means M&S's market share on fashion, home and beauty now sits at 10.2%, external for 2025-26.
Nnadi says M&S has been investing heavily in its retail spaces in recent years, focusing on "accessible luxury" with stores that feel "welcoming, new and fresh".
And that's something Clark has noticed too.
"Getting an iced coffee and having a walk around M&S with my friends is the perfect Saturday," she says. "My generation do so much sitting on our phones, so an in-person experience becomes a bit of an activity."
'I'm getting straight to M&S'
![Model Jodie Kidd presents a creation by M&S at the brand's SS27 catwalk show at London Fashion Week, in London, Britain, September 18, 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9660/live/c53ae580-b36b-11f1-8f19-bd786ea30d0b.jpg)
According to Sian, M&S has also taken "more risks" recently, which has helped it "create viral moments", including hosting a pit-lane fashion show at this year's F1 British Grand Prix and collaborating with British designers and creators.
"I'm seeing on Instagram or TikTok somebody say, 'Oh my goodness, this faux leather jacket is from M&S and it looks like it's Â£500 from the runway.'
"And what am I doing? I'm hop, skip, jumping into my car and getting straight to my local M&S to hunt it down," Sian jokes. "They have embraced young designers like Marco Capaldo, the founder and creative director of 16Arlington," adds Nnadi.
"And the Aries collab was genius and unexpected - it's a brand that has a lot of fashion kudos and is very British in its aesthetic but represents a younger vision of what British cool looks like," she says.
Clark agrees the brand has "homed in on experts in their craft, rather than partnering with a million different people" like other fashion brands have made the mistake of doing.
She notes their recent partnership with Stormzy's stylist Melissa Holbrook-Akposoe, who goes by Melissa's Wardrobe on social media, as "adding credibility" for younger shoppers.
More weekend picks
- ![A woman dressed in a black dress waves the back of the dress behind her on a catwalk in Trafalgar Square, with crowds either side of her watching on.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/c338/live/86c853f0-7aaa-11f0-919c-e1195b87955e.jpg)
  - Published17 August 2025
 ![Shoppers inside a Claire's store with rows of merchandise](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/dd41/live/7f8bb5a0-79fb-11f0-83cc-c5da98c419b8.jpg)
- ![Shoppers, not in focus, walk past a Primark store in London](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/a888/live/501dd8b0-86b2-11f1-8c61-e72dd81a46e3.jpg)
  - Published12 January 2025
 ![A woman sits at a sewing machine in a factory](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/ebaf/live/38f385a0-d1a4-11ef-87df-d575b9a434a4.jpg)
summary: Marks and Spencer (M&S) is successfully rebranding to attract shoppers under 35 while maintaining its core older audience through fresh marketing strategies and trendy designs. The retailer recently hosted its first-ever London Fashion Week show, featuring immediate-wear items inspired by its archives and contemporary high-fashion trends like barrel jeans and funnel necks. Experts attribute this shift to changing consumer habits favoring capsule wardrobes, quality staples, and strategic collaborations with designers and influencers.
key_points: M&S hosted its first-ever London Fashion Week show featuring archive-inspired archive collections available for immediate purchase.
The brand is successfully attracting younger shoppers under 35 by incorporating trendy styles like barrel jeans, faux fur jackets, and party wear.
Shifting consumer habits away from fast fashion toward durable capsule wardrobes and quality staples have helped M&S align with modern shopping preferences.
M&S has driven viral moments and built credibility through unexpected collaborations with designers and digital creators like Melissa Holbrook-Akposoe and Marco Capaldo.

title: Photographer Rankin: 'It feels like the old days - London is really happening'
author: Jessica Burrell
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![London’s Hidden Gems: Photobook Cafe in Shoreditch](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/10/19/Rankin.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![STYLE](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_style_embed_desktop.png)
Home is…
I live in Hampstead. Honestly, if you’d said to me three or four years ago, you’re going to be in Hampstead, I would have laughed at you because I have never thought of myself as somebody who would live there. Now, I’m like, “This is the best place I’ve ever lived.” It’s funny because I was born in Glasgow and they say that if you’re born there, you have the shortest average lifespan, whereas if you’re born in Hampstead, you have the longest. I hope I’ll be somewhere in the middle.
Where was your first flat in London?
Peckham. I went to the London College of Printing and my dad found some work for me in Peckham. I love the 53 bus and the Old Kent Road.
What was your first job ?
Coming out of college I started a magazine called Dazed & Confused. We used to borrow the Student Union Apple Mac equipment to work on it at the weekends. We very quickly realised that magazines weren’t going to pay much money, so Jefferson [Hack] and I got into the nightclub scene. We were both from outside London so it was a good way to build a community. I met pretty much all of the Dazed & Confused staff at nightclubs or parties.
“I get a bit irritated by people slagging off London. Every time I go out, it feels like the old days. London is really happening”
Where do you let your hair down?
I would probably go to the Groucho — it’s the only club I’m a member of. You always meet someone or bump into someone. I get a bit irritated by people, especially Americans, slagging off London. Every time I go out, it feels like the old days. London is really happening. There are more show openings — theatre, music, art. London has always had creative people, but this has got a lot to do with the Mayor and the openness to different types of people and the communities they build.
Who do you call when you want to have fun?
I don’t really phone people up. What happens is you go to a thing — it might be a gallery opening, a fashion party, a film premiere — and you meet people and it’s the unpredictability that’s the most exciting bit. Stephen Webster is always fun to bump into, or the other day I bumped into Rob Montgomery and Greta Bellamacina. It’s not necessarily the people you know the best.
What’s your favourite restaurant?
I would go to J Sheekey every day of the week. It’s where I’ve had the best meals. I love the Dover sole and the creamed spinach. I live near some really great pubs too: the Vine for good food and the Spaniards Inn for good vibes.
![J Sheekey, press handout](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/03/31/10/38/Copy-of-WH1_7812-copy-16-42-23.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Who is the most iconic Londoner?
I’m going to say two people: the Queen and McQueen. I think Queen Elizabeth II was the most amazing woman in the world. I got to photograph her and she was so extraordinary. She was so empowered and so funny — she really made me laugh. I knew Alexander McQueen and I think he was the epitome of how creative you can be as a Londoner.
What’s the best thing a cabbie has ever said to you?
When I say I’m a photographer, they always ask what I shoot. I say, “Oh, you know, portraits, famous people.” And the other day one cabbie replied, “It must be really hard.” I was like, “What do you mean?” and he goes, “Making those people look interesting.”
Who’s the best person you’ve photographed?
I say David Bowie, not because it’s my best shot, but because when I photographed him he made me realise that I should never presume anything about anyone. He walked into the room like he was Tigger from Winnie the Pooh and I had been expecting this cold, cool, distant guy. But he was so enthusiastic.
What’s your London secret?
I think going on the Thames Clipper is one of the most amazing things you can do. You can use your Oyster card on it. If I’ve got a couple of hours, I go to St Paul’s, go across the Millennium Bridge and then walk down the South Bank. You get to see a London that’s absolutely beautiful, that people have written songs about. That river is the one thing that holds us all together.
What’s your favourite place to see art in London?
The Rothko room in Tate Modern is probably my favourite. I love the Photographers’ Gallery. I actually really like Madame Tussauds as well. I think it’s such a laugh but when you’re a Londoner you don’t really go there, which is sad.
What are you up to for work?
I’m working on a new book called The Absurdity, about my journey into, and experiments with, artificial intelligence. I have my first show of generative work in France this month, called La F.AI.M. I’m also doing a book of my contact sheets, out next month.
As told to Jessica Burrell
Rankin is lead judge at the Abbey Road Music Photography Awards, which take place on September 24
summary: Photographer Rankin discusses his life in London, sharing his journey from living in Peckham and co-founding Dazed & Confused to currently residing in Hampstead. He praises London's vibrant arts and social scene, noting that the city feels as lively as it used to be. Rankin also shares personal reflections on his favorite local spots, memorable portrait subjects like David Bowie and Queen Elizabeth II, and his upcoming creative projects involving artificial intelligence.
key_points: Rankin co-founded the magazine Dazed & Confused shortly after coming out of college.
He believes London's current creative and social scene is thriving and feels like the old days.
He cites Queen Elizabeth II and Alexander McQueen as iconic Londoners.
David Bowie taught Rankin not to make presumptions about people after arriving to a photoshoot with great enthusiasm.
Rankin is currently working on a new book and generative art exhibition about artificial intelligence titled The Absurdity.

title: Harry Styles gives fans free coffee at his 'favourite' central London cafe
author: Holly Bishop
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Shania Twain shares her thoughts on potentially recording a duet with Harry Styles in the future](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/06/24/8/30/GettyImages-2264259728.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![The Weekender](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_weekender_embed_desktop.png)
Visitors to Kaffeine, which the As It Was singer called his “favourite coffee shop”, were told they need not pay as the bill had already been fronted by the star.
![Harry Styles has revealed new dates for his Together, Together tour (Doug Peters/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/14/35f71c74183db3102ef07c39d7dda313Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTMxMTg4-2.83682417.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Owner Peter Dore-Smith said he could not tell customers about the promotion on Saturday, September 12 ahead of time.
It was carried out at both the Great Titchfield Street and Eastcastle Street locations, which serve Australian-style coffee.
He said that he decorated the stores with Harry Styles posters and stickers, whilst staff wore ties to dress up like the artist, who visited one of the shops a couple of years ago.
When confused customers questioned why they did not need to pay, staff told them that they had been bought by Together, Together, the name of the artist's tour.
In a statement to fans, he said: ‘I love playing music, I love being with all of you and being a part of the love and joy you all create together every night. That’s why I wanted you to be the first to know we will be adding 2027 dates, which, honestly, at first I found daunting.
“Being an artist is the only life I've ever known really. I have been doing this since I was 16 years old, and I feel like the luckiest person in the world to still be sharing these moments with you.”
The star will perform 25 new dates next year, concluding with a final three nights in Wembley Stadium.
He will be joined by a series of special guests on select dates, including Kylie Minogue, LCD Soundsystem, Feist, Tears for Features, Tinashe and Lainey Wilsden.
summary: Pop star Harry Styles surprised visitors at his favorite central London cafe, Kaffeine, by paying for all of their coffee orders. The promotion took place across two locations decorated with posters and stickers of the singer, with staff dressing up in ties. The surprise coincided with the announcement of new 2027 tour dates for his Together, Together tour.
key_points: Harry Styles paid for customer coffee orders at his favorite central London cafe, Kaffeine.
The surprise event took place at both the Great Titchfield Street and Eastcastle Street locations.
Cafes were decorated with Harry Styles posters and stickers while staff wore ties.
Customers were informed by staff that their drinks were covered by the Together, Together tour.
The singer announced 25 new 2027 tour dates concluding with three nights at Wembley Stadium.

title: 14 London Openings To Know About This Season
author: Heather Steele
content:
![Triplebond](https://media.sheerluxe.com/fRdiKcEXuPVfwZgaaqmDdftnZDU=/800x0/smart/https%3A%2F%2Fsheerluxe.com%2Fsites%2Fsheerluxe%2Ffiles%2Farticles%2F2026%2F09%2Fsl-180926-new-openings-the-botree-hotel-marylebone-4.jpg) 
HOTELS
The Athenaeum, Mayfair
The Athenaeum has unveiled two new View Suites, created from the hotel’s former top-floor guest lounge. Overlooking Green Park, the spacious suites make the most of the hotel’s longstanding connection with the park, with sweeping views across the treetops offering an unexpected sense of the outdoors in the centre of London. Interiors strike a balance between the building’s art-deco heritage and a softer, more residential feel, with contemporary details bringing a fresh perspective to the historic property. The location is hard to beat too: Buckingham Palace, Bond Street, the Royal Academy and the West End are all within walking distance.
Visit ATHENAEUMHOTEL.COM
Claridge’s: Queen of Hotels, Hotel of Kings
One of London’s most iconic hotels has announced the publication of its first-ever book. Claridge’s: Queen of Hotels, Hotel of Kings offers an authorised account of how it became one of the world’s most celebrated hotels. Written by historian Martin Williams, the book draws on unprecedented access to Claridge’s archives to explore its history from its beginnings in 1812 to its place at the centre of modern London life. Expect plenty of glamour, famous names and behind-the-scenes stories, alongside an insight into how the hotel has continually reinvented itself while maintaining its reputation for traditional British hospitality. Over the years, Claridge’s has welcomed royalty, celebrities and some of the world’s most influential figures – and the book brings these chapters together to tell the story of a London landmark that has become almost as famous for its clientele as it is for its interiors and service. The book is available to preorder now.
Visit SHOP.CLARIDGES.CO.UK
Triplebond, Marylebone
Triplebond has opened at The BoTree in Marylebone, bringing together fitness, recovery, wellness and social spaces under one roof. The new members’ club includes Marylebone’s first rooftop pool alongside a rooftop Technogym gym, treatment spaces and a café on Marylebone Lane. At the core of the fitness offering is The Bassment, a music-led hot studio running classes across strength, barre, stretching, breathwork and higher-intensity sessions. Elsewhere, the Fire & Ice Circuit combines infrared sauna and cold-plunge therapy, while the Red Light Lounge focuses on recovery and jet-lag support. There’s also a Decompress Lounge with zero-gravity massage chairs and a Lymphatic Lounge created with Hyperice. For those after a more social approach to wellness, two floors of pool, terrace, bars and event spaces provide somewhere to linger, while the ground-floor café serves smoothies, juices, salads and wraps. Hotel guests can access the facilities alongside members.
Visit THEBOTREE.COM
![](https://media.sheerluxe.com/oGJ52P0iUz8OaCUh-lQBiz0wcO4=/800x0/smart/https%3A%2F%2Fsheerluxe.com%2Fsites%2Fsheerluxe%2Ffiles%2Farticles%2F2026%2F09%2Ftriplebond-the-atheanean.jpg) 
Daniel Galvin x The Beaumont, Mayfair
The Beaumont Mayfair has teamed up with renowned hairstylist Daniel Galvin to offer hotel guests a useful new perk. Guests staying at the hotel can access exclusive discounts at Daniel Galvin’s London salons or arrange for a senior stylist to come directly to their suite for a cut, blow-dry, styling session or treatment. For appointments at the flagship salon on George Street, the hotel can also arrange its private, chauffeur-driven courtesy car. The collaboration is designed with time-pressed travellers in mind, particularly those visiting London for an important event and wanting to organise their hair without adding another journey to the itinerary.
Visit THEBEAUMONT.COM
The Landmark London
The Landmark London has completed a major expansion of its wellness offering with the opening of a 710sq m spa in Marylebone. Designed by Alex Kravetz Design, the new space combines a sophisticated thermal suite with treatment rooms, relaxation areas and a selection of advanced skincare treatments. The thermal experience includes a 34°C vitality pool with hydrotherapy jets, aromatic steam room, Finnish sauna, ice fountain, heated marble loungers and multi-sensory showers, creating a comprehensive heat-and-cold circuit. There are also new day packages, ranging from two-hour thermal experiences to longer combinations of treatments, dining and hotel access. Four treatment rooms and a double treatment suite offer space for individual and shared experiences, while skincare partners include QMS Medicosmetics, Ashmira Botanica and OSKIA. Treatments range from high-performance facials to collagen-focused therapies.
Visit LANDMARKLONDON.CO.UK
![Triplebond, Ryan Wicks](<https://media.sheerluxe.com/pbKBUyEtf5gUv-OekniU3shy150=/1920x0/smart/filters:no_upscale()/https%3A%2F%2Fsheerluxe.com%2Fsites%2Fsheerluxe%2Ffiles%2Farticles%2F2026%2F09%2Fsl-180926-new-openings-the-botree-hotel-marylebone-1.jpg>) 
RESTAURANTS & BARS
Venus Bar at Brasserie Olivia, Chelsea
Brasserie Olivia is taking its French Riviera-inspired dining experience into the evening with the opening of Venus Bar on 9th October. Hidden downstairs via the Sloane Square brasserie’s grand wooden staircase, the new speakeasy-style bar will swap the restaurant’s light Riviera mood for something more 1970s-inspired. Designed by B3 Designers, the space features warm oak panelling, antique objects sourced from French markets, vintage vinyl and chartreuse velvet chairs, while a chrome bar takes centre stage. The music collection spans French female singers from the 1940s to the 1980s, rock and classical, with guests able to choose what’s played. Cocktails, created under the guidance of bartender Jennifer Le Nechet, take an experimental approach, from a cucumber and gin milk punch to a tomato-infused negroni. There will also be around 75 French wines, alongside brasserie snacks including oysters and gougères.
Visit LANOUVELLEGARDE.COM
The Pem, St James's
Award-winning chef, broadcaster and cookbook author Romy Gill MBE returns to the kitchen this month as she takes over The Pem at Conrad London St James. Her first permanent restaurant in six years, the new chapter will showcase regional Indian cooking inspired by Gill's upbringing and travels across the country. The menu spans the rich flavours of Punjab, Kerala's fragrant coastal cuisine and the vibrant street food of Bengal, with standout dishes including hand-dived scallops with raw mango, tandoori quail, Kashmiri morel lamb and Romy's celebrated butter chicken. On the drinks front, expect Indian-inspired cocktails and single-estate teas from Himachal Pradesh.
Visit ROMYGILLATTHEPEM.COM
Nettle, Covent Garden
Nettle is the new London restaurant from chef, farmer and Acre founder Will Devlin. Set on the fifth-floor rooftop of The Conduit in Covent Garden, it combines skyline views with an open-air garden and a fire kitchen centred around a custom-built charcoal grill. The menu follows Devlin’s farm-to-table approach, with much of the produce coming from his farm and Block Butchery at Spratsbourne Farm in Kent. Expect seasonal, fire-cooked dishes across snacks, small plates, larger dishes and sharing plates, with meat sourced through the restaurant’s whole-animal approach and responsibly caught British seafood. Dishes include Acre charcuterie, hake croquettes, wild rabbit skewers, wild venison and Kent lamb, alongside plenty of vegetables treated as a main event rather than an afterthought.
Visit NETTLE-RESTAURANT.CO.UK
![Brasserie Olivia](<https://media.sheerluxe.com/7sBaCyzNuwzcqIKigAtHe8oIldA=/1920x0/smart/filters:no_upscale()/https%3A%2F%2Fsheerluxe.com%2Fsites%2Fsheerluxe%2Ffiles%2Farticles%2F2026%2F09%2Fbrasserie-olivia-london-joannpai-08467.jpg>) 
Dockley Road, Bermondsey
Tucked into the south-west corner of Spa Terminus, Dockley Road is a neighbourhood restaurant, café and bar built around the produce and specialist suppliers of Bermondsey’s food district. The menu changes almost daily, shaped by what’s available from the surrounding butchers, fishmongers, greengrocers, cheesemongers and wine merchants. The cooking is broadly British and European, with a focus on simple dishes that let good ingredients do the work. There’s also a strong whole-animal approach, with beef used nose-to-tail across steaks, burgers, pies, braises and ragu. Recent dishes include roast cod with Provençal vegetables and Dillay Dexter ragu with pappardelle, while weekend breakfast brings Turkish eggs, scallop and bacon baps and smoked haddock kedgeree.
Visit DOCKLEYROAD.CO.UK
The Emory Rooftop Bar, Knightsbridge
The Emory’s rooftop bar has unveiled The View, a new cocktail menu inspired by the London landmarks visible from its spectacular 360º vantage point. Created in collaboration with renowned Argentinian bartender Renato ‘Tato’ Giovannoni, the menu brings together Argentine ingredients, spirits and flavours with the bar team’s own contemporary approach. A total of 12 signature cocktails have been designed around different perspectives of the capital, with familiar classics reworked in increasingly unexpected ways. The Alignment, for example, takes its cue from a French 75, combining Renais Gin, passion berries, Champagne and tropical fruit cordial, while The Layer is a Paloma-style drink made with Mijenta Reposado Tequila, pimentón de cachi, corn and grapefruit.
Visit MAYBOURNE.COM
Celeste, Notting Hill
Celeste is the third property from the team behind Estelle Manor, bringing a private members’ club to Notting Hill with an all-day Italian-American restaurant at its centre. Members have access to all four floors of the Notting Hill townhouse, with plenty to discover beyond the restaurant. Upstairs, the Members’ Bar provides a more intimate setting for drinks, while a Japanese restaurant adds another dining option. There are also private spaces designed to work equally well for a few hours of quiet work during the day or drinks and gatherings in the evening. The ground floor is open to everyone, with an al fresco terrace for morning coffee, an elegant bar and a light-filled dining room offering both counter seating and generous tables. We like the pretty Courtyard at the back of the restaurant. Menu highlights include king crab tagliolini, nettle and ricotta bottoni, and a caesar wedge salad.
Visit CELESTENOTTINGHILL.COM
![Celeste](<https://media.sheerluxe.com/EdZRnTiO6Yrzzw990wCNx-iTLQI=/1920x0/smart/filters:no_upscale()/https%3A%2F%2Fsheerluxe.com%2Fsites%2Fsheerluxe%2Ffiles%2Farticles%2F2026%2F09%2Fsl-180926-london-openings-celeste-restaurant-the-courtyard-landscape.jpg>) 
Alba, Knightsbridge
Harrods has a new dining hotspot. Ten-seat omakase restaurant Alba is putting the focus firmly on the quality of its ingredients. Drawing on the Japanese and Italian appreciation for sea urchin – known as uni in Japan and ricci di mare in Italy – the experience, which is led by head chef Takuya Kaneko of Zuma, celebrates seafood at its freshest. Expect hand-selected uni, otoro, caviar and the day’s catch, served course by course directly in front of you. There’s no set menu to consult in advance: instead, dishes are dictated by what the sea has delivered that morning and the chef’s judgement on how best to serve it.
Visit ALBA-LDN.UK
Room 86 at Moi, Soho
Moi’s former Listening Room has been reimagined as Room 86, bringing a renewed focus to its combination of music, cocktails and late-night drinking. The subterranean space retains its intimate, music-led atmosphere, but now has a new DJ programme built around five distinct nights. Tuesdays will focus on Old School Hip Hop and experimental sounds, Wednesdays on Funky House, Thursdays on Deep House with a curated sake pairing, and Fridays and Saturdays on Groovy House. Guests can arrive through the dedicated Wardour Street entrance or continue their evening here after dinner at Moi. Alongside the music, the bar serves cocktails, wine and sake, with snacks from the Moi kitchen available throughout the night.
Visit MOIRESTAURANT.COM
Café 22, Mayfair
Café 22 is the new restaurant at The Twenty Two on North Audley Street, with a fresh look, new menu and drinks list overseen by Guillaume Glipa, formerly of Chiltern Firehouse, Louie London and Annabel’s. The menu focuses on French classics, from canard à l’orange and poulet rôti à la truffe to whole grilled sea bass, crispy potatoes and sauce vierge. Desserts are nostalgic, with brown butter madeleines, tarte tatin, crème brûlée and profiteroles all making an appearance. The redesigned interiors combine rich, grounded tones with lighter neutrals, bringing together classic Mayfair elegance and a more relaxed Parisian feel, alongside a rotating artist-in-residence programme. Drinks are equally central to the experience, with a roaming martini trolley bringing some tableside theatre, plus champagne cocktails, a French 75-inspired serve and highballs.
Visit THETWENTYTWO.COM
![Alba](https://media.sheerluxe.com/HsmzoqMiFS6TICyG1qwFNzxWwMM=/800x0/smart/https%3A%2F%2Fsheerluxe.com%2Fsites%2Fsheerluxe%2Ffiles%2Farticles%2F2026%2F09%2Fsl-180926-new-openings-alba-london-italian-japanese-restaurant_0.jpg)
summary: London is seeing a wave of new hotel, wellness, restaurant, and bar openings this season. Notable debuts include updated luxury suites and amenities at high-end hotels like The Athenaeum and The Landmark, innovative private wellness clubs such as Triplebond, and diverse dining experiences ranging from regional Indian cuisine at The Pem to the intimate omakase spot Alba at Harrods. Additionally, historic institutions like Claridge's are branching out by publishing their first authorized books.
key_points: The Athenaeum in Mayfair has opened two new View Suites overlooking Green Park.
Triplebond at The BoTree in Marylebone features a rooftop pool, fitness facilities, and an extensive wellness circuit.
Chef Romy Gill MBE has taken over the kitchen at The Pem to offer regional Indian cuisine.
Harrods has introduced Alba, an exclusive ten-seat omakase restaurant led by head chef Takuya Kaneko.
Claridge's announced the publication of its first-ever authorised book detailing its history since 1812.

title: London-Stevenage rail services disrupted by electricity fault
author: Rachael McMenemy
content:
![An LNER-branded train at a platform.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/4fdd/live/3fecf8e0-b326-11f1-a6b1-91735b4529e5.jpg)
LNER services are among those affected by the issue
- Published
An electricity supply failure has caused major disruption to rail services.
The fault occurred in Welwyn Garden City and is causing problems for services running between London's Finsbury Park and Stevenage.
LNER services between London King's Cross and Peterborough, as well as Thameslink and Great Northern services, are subject to delays and cancellations.
Network Rail and electricity suppliers are dealing with the fault, and disruption is expected until 15:00 BST.
LNER customers are advised to check if their tickets are valid on other services. A full list is available on its website, external.
National Rail said services, external that run between King's Lynn and London King's Cross would run between King's Lynn and Cambridge only.
Alternative trains to Cambridge are available from Ely.
There will also be a reduced Great Northern service between Cambridge and London but tickets from Cambridge will be accepted on Thameslink services to London St Pancras International, Great Northern services to London King's Cross, and Greater Anglia services to London Liverpool Street.
Great Northern will be operating a reduced service at peak times from Peterborough to London.
There will also be a reduced peak-time service between Hertford North and Moorgate, National Rail said.
Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.
summary: An electricity supply failure in Welwyn Garden City has caused significant delays and cancellations for rail services between London's Finsbury Park and Stevenage. Affected operators include LNER, Thameslink, and Great Northern, with disruption expected to last until 15:00 BST. Network Rail and electricity suppliers are currently addressing the fault.
key_points: An electricity supply failure in Welwyn Garden City disrupted rail services between Finsbury Park and Stevenage.
LNER, Thameslink, and Great Northern services are experiencing delays and cancellations.
Network Rail and electricity suppliers are responding to the fault, with disruption expected until 15:00 BST.
Various altered routes, reduced peak services, and ticket acceptance arrangements on alternative lines have been put in place.

title: Singer Harry Styles funds free coffee at two London cafes
author: Emma Lennox; Sally Garster
content:
![Four people smile at the camera, three wearing ties. One faces away from the camera wearing a Together, Together tour t-shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/d8d3/live/466968e0-b27f-11f1-94d0-89db86965db8.jpg)
Owner Peter Dore-Smith said his coffee shops were a "favourite" of Harry Styles
- Published
Harry Styles bought coffees for all of the visitors to his "favourite" London coffee shop to celebrate the extension of his record-breaking Together, Together tour.
The singer funded free coffees for all of the customers at Kaffeine's two central London cafes on Saturday through promoter Live Nation.
Owner Peter Dore-Smith said he was not allowed to promote the free drinks on social media, but could tell customers that they had been bought by Together, Together, the name of the artist's tour.
Last week Styles announced three additional dates at Wembley Stadium on 25, 27 and 28 August 2027.
![A receipt from the cafe which has the total price of an iced flat white of Â£4.80 reduced to Â£0 with the 100% discount from Together Together.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/d587/live/54826b20-b27f-11f1-94d0-89db86965db8.jpg)
Customers were told their drinks had been paid for by Together, Together
Dore-Smith said he was told by Live Nation that his company was chosen as Styles' "favourite coffee shop", but the free drinks could not be promoted beforehand.
The owner said Styles covered the usual Saturday takings at both sites on Eastcastle Street and Great Titchfield Street and also added a buffer to ensure all drinks could be paid for.
Dore-Smith said that the star had visited his Eastcastle Street coffee shop "a couple of years ago", and that they put his song lyrics on their blackboard during his last concerts in London.
On the day of the giveaway, Dore-Smith said they placed posters in the window and put Together, Together tour stickers provided by the promoter on every cup of coffee they sold.
Styles' music played in the shops and staff wore ties to "dress up" like the artist, who often performs wearing the accessory.
"We put extra staff on, and on the day people just rocked up as normal," Dore-Smith said.
When customers asked why their drink was free, his staff told them "because Harry Styles is buying everyone's coffee today," he said.
He added: "I know they've done it with a florist before, and I think they've done it with an ice cream parlour before."
Live Nation declined to comment.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: Singer Harry Styles funded free coffee for all customers at two central London cafes operated by Kaffeine on Saturday. The giveaway celebrated the extension of his Together, Together tour, which recently added three new dates at Wembley Stadium. Cafe owner Peter Dore-Smith stated that the promotion could not be announced beforehand and covered the usual Saturday sales plus a financial buffer.
key_points: Harry Styles funded free coffee at Kaffeine's two central London locations on Saturday.
The promotion celebrated the extension of his Together, Together tour, including new Wembley Stadium dates.
Cafe owner Peter Dore-Smith was prohibited from promoting the free drinks on social media beforehand.
Staff wore ties and played Styles' music to celebrate the event while using tour-branded cup stickers.

title: Harry gives speech at first public appearance since return to UK
author: Jordan Reynolds
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/18/00/11328cfed2510fd81934bfc52ef6e0baY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5NzczMTc1-2.85886811.jpg?crop=8:5,smart&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
The Duke of Sussex posed for photos and gave a speech during his first public appearance since returning to the UK.
At a champagne reception in an adjoining courtyard, he told guests he was “incredibly excited” to meet the winners and nominees after being part of the judging panel, alongside the Duchess of Sussex, for the awards.
The ceremony aims to honour the remarkable feats of extraordinary people and organisations at the heart of the global Invictus community.
After welcoming Harry with a hug, Sonique, who was DJing at the bash, said: “It’s nice to have him home. He used to come to my gigs, I have missed him.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/22/068d36106c4555bf5e0e8f4b3f9f87f0Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5NzY3NTA1-2.85886624.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The pair posed for pictures at a specially erected photo booth before the duke was taken into the awards.
The evening recognised those who have beaten the odds, supported others in their recovery, advanced sport and rehabilitation, or made an outstanding contribution to the wider Invictus community.
The award categories recognise resilience, community, commitment to international sports recovery and philanthropic support.
Giving a speech at the awards, Harry told the story of how Invictus began.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/19/a13b8aab19b9ca1b95c058511cd4eee0Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5NzUzNjM5-2.85886636.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
He said: “In 2008, flying home from Afghanistan, I travelled alongside three seriously injured British servicemen and the coffin of a Danish soldier.
Read More
“That flight stayed with me because it helped me begin to understand two things about the military that would shape the rest of my life: it gives you purpose, identity, belonging, a team; and in a matter of seconds, injury or illness can take it all away.
“Years later, after seeing the Warrior Games in America, we brought an idea back to London. We had less than a year to make it happen — which was probably useful, because it gave everyone less time to tell us it couldn’t be done.
“In September 2014, more than 400 competitors from 13 nations came together for the first ever Invictus Games. Now 12 years later, thousands have benefited. We have 26 nations in our community, and the games are coming home!
“And something happened that was bigger than sports competition. People who thought a part of their life was over began to see that something else might just be beginning. Their families, too, saw loved ones return to them in mind and spirit.”
The duke also had a message to veterans at the awards and around the world.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/22/166e56d95ff34bba2ab56949cf90283aY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5NzY3NjA4-2.85887098.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
He said: “And to the veterans here tonight, and those wherever you are around the world, I want to say this as one soldier to another: your service matters. What you gave in uniform matters. And people far beyond the military community who see in your example what courage, resilience and leadership actually look like.
“People are watching. The teammate who is struggling. The young soldier wondering what life after uniform might look like. The family trying to find its way forward.
“You may no longer wear the uniform, but you still lead. Every time you get back up, reach back for someone else, or turn what happened to you into purpose for others, you are serving again — just differently.
“And that matters far beyond our military community. National resilience isn’t built by governments alone. It is built in communities – by people who know how to endure, adapt, lead under pressure and look after one another when things get tough.
“At a time when societies around the world are being tested, the Invictus spirit has something to teach all of us. This community doesn’t just demonstrate resilience. It helps build it.
“Never underestimate what your example gives to the world.”
Harry founded the Invictus Games for wounded, injured and sick military personnel and veterans, which takes place every two years, in 2014.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/20/be109fb9f2f7ebf5fdc5607af551aa64Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5NzU4MDA5-2.85886968.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The next edition in 2027 represents a homecoming not only for the duke, but the games, with Birmingham named as the host city.
Harry’s first public engagement since moving back to the UK from the US came after a war of words broke out between his father the King and Earl Charles Spencer, the brother of his late mother, Diana, Princess of Wales.
It comes after explosive claims from a new memoir by Earl Spencer were published, in which the King is said to have told Diana’s brother at the time of her death in 1997 that “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”.
A palace spokesman said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”
Meanwhile, this week it was revealed that Harry and Meghan moved their children to a new school after talks with their security team.
Prince Archie, seven, and five-year-old Princess Lilibet had only just started at their new school in England after the family relocated from the US three weeks ago.
But they will now join another one, after heavy traffic and the lengthy journey to the school reportedly put the Sussexes’ security team under strain, Hello! magazine reported.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/22/caf048a4753b64fd34d6da7742727371Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5NzY3Njcw-2.85886789.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The decision comes amid reports that both the Sussexes will receive an official risk assessment following their return.
In January 2020, Harry and Meghan had announced they intended to step back as “senior” members of the royal family, become financially independent, still support Queen Elizabeth II, but split their time between the UK and North America.
But the late Queen ruled at the Sandringham Summit, which was convened to resolve the Megxit crisis, that the couple could not be half in and half out – and the King recently said the agreement still stands.
summary: The Duke of Sussex made his first public appearance since returning to the UK by giving a speech at an awards ceremony celebrating the global Invictus community. During his speech, Harry reflected on the origins of the Invictus Games and praised the ongoing resilience and leadership of veterans. His return coincides with recent family developments, including reports about a new school for his children and ongoing discussions regarding royal security and living arrangements.
key_points: Prince Harry gave a speech at an awards ceremony honoring members and organizations of the global Invictus community during his first public appearance since returning to the UK.
He shared the founding story of the Invictus Games, tracing it back to a 2008 flight from Afghanistan and the Warrior Games in America.
The duke delivered a message to veterans emphasizing that their service and resilience continue to matter beyond the military community.
The 2027 Invictus Games will be hosted in Birmingham, marking a homecoming for the games.
Harry and Meghan reportedly moved their children to a new school following security concerns and long journey times.

title: Human remains found in woodland belong to mother who went missing seven years ago
author: Ted Hennessey
content:
Police have confirmed that human remains found in woodland in southwest London following a wildfire are those of a Southampton mother-of-three who went missing nearly seven years ago.
The Metropolitan Police were called on the evening of 12 August after bones, thought to belong to a woman aged between 25 and 45, were found near Padstow Walk in Feltham after the area was affected by a fire.
Detectives had launched a murder investigation, but Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary have now taken over the probe after the remains were identified as those of Joanne Sheen, the Press Association has learned.
A 56-year-old man from Southampton was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder on Thursday, and remains in police custody.
Sheen, 44, had not been seen since she travelled from Fareham, Hampshire, heading to her home city of Southampton, on 5 December 2019.
She was reported missing by her family in February 2020.
![Police were called to the woodland area last month](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/17/14/01M0JGK31YFYPKS5QYK2W88XDW.jpg)
The discovery came after extensive forensic examination and DNA testing of the remains.
A Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary spokesperson told PA that more than 4,000 lines of enquiry have been raised, more than 300 statements taken, and detailed searches carried out at more than 10 addresses and on numerous vessels.
Specialist teams have also searched waterways and woodland around Southampton.
The spokesperson added: “As part of our investigation, we have today arrested a 56-year-old man from Southampton on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder. He remains in custody at this time as our enquiries continue.
“As our investigation enters this next stage, we are working closely with our colleagues in the Metropolitan Police to establish exactly what happened to Joanne.
“Her death is being treated as murder, and we remain committed to identifying and bringing those responsible to justice.”
Detective Chief Inspector Toby Elcock, from the major crime team, said: “This is a significant development in what has been a long and complex investigation and provides us with several new lines of enquiry, which we are exploring with our dedicated team.
“While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne’s family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty.
“Throughout this investigation, Joanne’s family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time.
![Police tape near to the scene, where a member of the public found human remains in woodland in Feltham, southwest London](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/21/16/01M0JDRB09J4C9ZN5V4GN75CCN.jpg)
“As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable.
“There may still be people who have information about Joanne’s disappearance, her movements before she went missing, or how she came to be in Feltham.
“The passage of time does not lessen the importance of that information. No matter how small or insignificant it may seem, we would urge anyone who may know something to come forward.
“We understand that coming forward may feel difficult, particularly if you are worried about the consequences, but we are asking you to think about the family who are left without their loved one and who are waiting for answers. Please do the right thing. If you know something, now is the time to come forward.
“We are also pleased that Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate its £20,000 reward offer in support of our investigation. If anyone has information but does not feel comfortable speaking directly to police, I would encourage them to contact Crimestoppers anonymously.”
A Metropolitan Police spokesman confirmed that the remains were found by a member of the public after the nearby land was affected by a recent wildfire.
The site is close to Bedfont Lakes Country Park.
summary: Police have confirmed that human remains found in a southwest London woodland following a wildfire belong to Joanne Sheen, a mother-of-three from Southampton who went missing in December 2019. Following the identification, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary took over the investigation, treating her death as murder. A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and remains in police custody.
key_points: Human remains discovered in a Feltham woodland after a wildfire were identified as missing mother Joanne Sheen through DNA testing.
Sheen had been missing since December 2019 and was reported missing by her family in February 2020.
A 56-year-old man from Southampton was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and remains in custody.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary have taken over the murder investigation, working alongside the Metropolitan Police.
Crimestoppers has reinstated a £20,000 reward for information related to the case.

title: PETA protestors invade catwalk at London Fashion Week
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Peta protesters interrupt H&M LFW show](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/19/11/PETA-protest-LFW.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) The audience members jumped onto the catwalk in stages, with the first within the first couple of minutes of the start of the show. One of the protestors even managed to get backstage, walking out with the models. ![

LFW week protest PETA H&M

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/20/00/LFW-week-protest-PETA-HM.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Each protestor was able to walk the full length of the runway before security intervened, following them along the stage, with each protester leaving without any physical struggle. The protestors caused a hubbub in the crowd, with the actual collection completely overshadowed by the spectacle. It comes just days after a fashion CEO has apologized after restraining two protesters at a New York Fashion Week show. Steven Kolb, CEO and President of the Council of Fashion Designers, grabbed a protester at the COS fashion show on Sunday. Footage showed Kolb gripping one PETA protester by his face, covering his mouth as he shouted a slogan, and also dragging a female protester to the ground and placing a leg over her body.
summary: PETA protestors interrupted an H&M show at London Fashion Week by invading the catwalk in stages, with one even making it backstage. Security eventually intervened, allowing each protester to walk the full length of the runway before leaving without a struggle. The demonstration overshadowed the fashion collection, occurring just days after New York Fashion Exchange CEO Steven Kolb physically restrained two PETA protesters at a fashion show.
key_points: PETA protestors interrupted the H&M fashion show at London Fashion Week.
Protestors walked the full length of the runway and one even got backstage before security intervened.
The demonstration completely overshadowed the fashion collection being presented.
The incident follows a recent event where fashion CEO Steven Kolb restrained two PETA protestors at a New York Fashion Week show.

title: Historic north London pub to reopen as comedy and cabaret venue
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![The London Question: How can Sadiq Khan stop pubs from closing?](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/15/00/Screenshot-2026-09-17-164436.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Martin Besserman, a Crouch End resident who runs the Monkey Business Comedy Club, is taking over the venue for at least three shows this autumn.
"We’ll be bringing you a series of exciting Saturday night pop-up comedy and cabaret shows, with fabulous performers, great entertainment, food and a fully stocked bar.
"The Dairy has been closed for the past few weeks, so we’re thrilled to be bringing this fantastic space back to life with a series of one-off pop-up nights."
The first events will take place on October 31, November 28 and December 12 - with lineups and more dates to be announced.
A "high percentage" of money raised will go towards community projects and charitable causes.
The Old Dairy, a Grade II listed pub, closed during lockdown when it was taken over by squatters.
The pub has decorative panels illustrating traditional milk production methods, a nod to the site originally serving as a shop and creamery for the Friern Manor Dairy Farm Company in the 19th century.
Built in 1890, the building once housed stables and cowsheds, and the outside wall has large panels depicting all stages of the milk production process, from cows grazing to the milk being delivered.
The site remained a dairy until the 1960s. It was bought by Regent Inns in 1997 and converted into a pub, and was later sold to Real Pubs and then Greene King in 2011.
More details about the cabaret events, including line-ups and ticket information, are expected to be released soon via the Finsbury Park Cabaret Facebook page.
summary: The historic Grade II listed Old Dairy pub in north London, which closed during lockdown, is reopening for a series of pop-up comedy and cabaret shows this autumn. Run by Martin Besserman of the Monkey Business Comedy Club, the events will support community projects and charitable causes. The building originally served as a 19th-century creamery and dairy before being converted into a pub in 1997.
key_points: The Old Dairy is reopening as a comedy and cabaret venue starting this autumn.
Events are scheduled for October 31, November 28, and December 12.
A high percentage of the money raised will go to community projects and charities.
The 1890 building originally operated as a shop and creamery before becoming a pub in 1997.
The pub closed during lockdown after being taken over by squatters.

title: Notting Hill pub faces licence battle after resident moans about 'vertical drinking'
author: Katherine Gray
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![No standing at Soho pubs and bars? Londoners react to council's proposals](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/9/52/Screenshot_2026-09-15_130032.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
The Champion, located close to Hyde Park, was previously known as one of London’s iconic gay pubs.
Now the premises is facing a licence review, after a local resident complained that the pub’s customers were blocking the public highway while drinking outside.
The irritated resident has asked the council to force the venue to ensure any drinking outside is only permitted while seated from plastic containers.
“Patrons regularly congregate outside the premises, generating noise and disturbance for local residents, particularly during evening hours,” he wrote in a council report.
“I have raised these concerns directly with staff on multiple occasions and requested that music volumes be reduced and furniture relocated within the permitted area. Despite these requests, the issues have continued.”
![The Champion in Notting Hill](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/17/9/52/Screenshot_2026-09-15_130032.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Steel also alleged that drinking glasses and, on occasion, broken glass, had been found on the mews adjacent to the pub.
“The presence of discarded glassware and broken glass presents a foreseeable risk of injury to children, as are intoxicated individuals blocking the highway. My child has previously come close to direct contact with broken glass in the vicinity of the premises,” he wrote.
In total one person supported the review application and five wrote in support of the premise.
“As the area has changed so dramatically over the years, it has remained a welcoming meeting place for local residents and visitors alike, helping to preserve the character and sense of community that once defined the neighbourhood.”
Alexander Nandris, General Manager at the pub, said that neither of the two flats above the pub had complained about the premise.
Read More
He said that staff undertake regular checks of the pavement to ensure there is no glass outside and that customers are not drinking in unlicensed areas.
summary: The Champion pub in Notting Hill is facing a licence review after a local resident complained about noise, blocked public highways, and discarded glassware. The complainant requested that outdoor drinking be restricted to seated patrons using plastic containers. Meanwhile, the pub's general manager defended the venue, noting that staff conduct regular checks of the pavement and that neither of the flats directly above the pub has complained.
key_points: The Champion pub is facing a licence review following a complaint from a local resident.
The resident cited noise, blocked public roads from 'vertical drinking', and dangerous broken glass near the premises.
The complainant asked the council to force the pub to restrict outdoor drinking to seated customers using plastic containers.
Five people wrote in support of the venue, highlighting its role in preserving neighborhood character.
The pub's general manager stated that staff regularly check the pavement for glass and unlicensed drinking areas, and noted that residents living directly above the pub have not complained.

title: Cast announced for Club NVRLND musical in London
author: Alex Wood
content:
![Immersive Peter Pan nightclub musical Club NVRLND announces casting](https://www.whatsonstage.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/07/Thomas-Grant-and-Martha-Kirby.jpg?w=100) 
Diana Vickers and Le Fil are to star in Club NVRLND, which will transfer to the Vaults in Waterloo following a sold-out run at the 2025 Edinburgh Festival Fringe.
Vickers will play Wendy Darling, with Le Fil returning as Tiger Lily. Matthew Gent will reprise his role as Hook, while Ian Oswald will play The Crocodile. Becky Bassett will play Ensemble/Nana and Damian Buhagiar will play Ensemble/Smee.
The cast also includes Max James Hodge, Joshua De La-Garde, Elinor Morris, Ashley-Jordon Packer, Appolilly Szwarc and Natalie Yin. Further casting is to be announced. The production will run from 14 November 2026 to 31 January 2027.
Conceived and directed by Steven Kunis, with a book by Olivier Award-winning Jack Holden, Club NVRLND is an immersive nightclub musical based on Peter Pan. Audiences enter NVRLND, where the story unfolds around them as they drink, dance and party alongside the cast.
The production features music by artists including Britney Spears, Rihanna, Lady Gaga, Kylie Minogue, P!nk, Coldplay, Outkast, Avril Lavigne, Jennifer Lopez, Christina Aguilera, Katy Perry and Panic! At the Disco. The doors open an hour before the performance, with the party continuing afterwards.The creative team includes choreographer Ashley Nottingham, executive music producer and arranger Hugo Dunn-Vereker, set and costume designer Suzu Sakai, lighting designer Robbie Butler, sound designer Sound Quiet Time, casting director Lucy Casson, music producer and arranger Liam James, vocal arranger Simon Nathan, music supervisor Colm O’Regan and creative producer Aida Rocci.
Club NVRLND is produced by David Adkin, RJG Productions, Midnight Theatricals and Ley Line Entertainment in association with NewYorkRep, People and Golden Wax Productions. It is presented by arrangement with Great Ormond Street Hospital Children’s Charity and Concord Theatricals Ltd.
Vickers will appear at all performances in November and December and on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays in January.
summary: The immersive Peter Pan nightclub musical "Club NVRLND" has announced its cast for an upcoming London run at the Vaults in Waterloo, following a sold-out run at the 2025 Edinburgh Festival Fringe. Diana Vickers and Le Fil will star as Wendy Darling and Tiger Lily, respectively, alongside other cast members including Matthew Gent as Hook and Ian Oswald as The Crocodile. Conceived and directed by Steven Kunis with a book by Jack Holden, the production runs from 14 November 2026 to 31 January 2027.
key_points: Diana Vickers and Le Fil will star in Club NVRLND as Wendy Darling and Tiger Lily.
The production is an immersive Peter Pan nightclub musical where audiences drink, dance, and party alongside the cast.
Performances are scheduled to run from 14 November 2026 to 31 January 2027 at the Vaults in Waterloo.
The show features popular music from artists such as Britney Spears, Rihanna, Lady Gaga, and Katy Perry.

title: Why is London's mobile phone reception getting worse?
author: Shakira Abdi; BBC England Data Unit
content:
![A mobile phone screen showing a no signal sign from a Google page.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/fea9/live/987a3970-ad4d-11f1-8963-d14e6edce0d0.jpg)
Independent data analysed by Which? showed that over a third of customers in the UK reported problems with poor signal.
- Published
London's mobile phone connectivity "continues to lag frustratingly behind other international hubs" Mobile UK, which represents several network providers, has said.
Its comments come as the latest global rankings for internet speeds, external showed London had fallen to 91st place, five places lower than last month.
Data commissioned by the BBC England Data Unit found some of the worst areas were Liverpool Street and Covent Garden, where service proved to be extremely slow and unreliable during commuter peak rush hours but worked normally during quiet mornings.
So what impact does this this lack of connectivity have on Londoners and their ability to earn a living and what are the reasons behind it?
New developments vs antenna sites
Once a development receives planning consent, mobile operators are issued a notice-to-quit (NTQ) to remove their antennas.
They are given an 18-month notice period to find a new site but finding new antenna sites can take an average of two years. Temporary sites also need to be found to maintain signal coverage.
Virgin Media 02 recently called for urgent reform after being "forced" to switch off dozens of mobile sites across London because of new developments.
Robert Joyce , director of mobile access engineering at Virgin Media O2, said: "If we can't find a replacement site before we remove that equipment then we can have a coverage hole in that location."
![Google maps view of Charing Cross Road, Earlham Street and King Street highlighted in red.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1408/cpsprodpb/83cc/live/6da863e0-b0d9-11f1-b427-b9b4ddc559ae.png)
A survey taken near Covent Garden found that almost every mobile data test across four UK networks had failed
Operators say that thousands of people can be affected when a site is lost and cannot be replaced.
Mobile UK, which represents EE, O2, Three and Vodafone, added: "Delivering world-class coverage is an uphill battle in a high-density city where development constantly reshapes the skyline."
Coverage or capacity?
Network capacity is the total amount of data a network can handle at any given time.
Mobile users can have four or five signal bars but still experience slow uploads, undelivered messages and failed calls when a network is congested.
Network surveyor Philip Maguire, 63, and founder/CEO of Inakalum, said: "When the areas are busy very often the networks don't have enough capacity to deal with all the data demands from users, and that's a capacity issue not a signal problem."
He added that most people would have "no chance" finding a reliable connection in the evening after leaving work despite the signal working in the early morning.
![A man wearing a blue jacket with a white logo. In the background this a shoe rack with multiple trainers, a stack of boxes on the left and a desk with other belongings on the right.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/fedd/live/862bcae0-ad4d-11f1-8963-d14e6edce0d0.jpg)
Londoners complain that poor mobile service is not only impacting their social life, but also their professional work
Philip surveyed three streets on behalf of the England Data Unit, all within a few minutes' walk of Covent Garden on a weekday evening. He found that more than one in four data tests failed outright for EE, O2, Three and Vodafone.
Even when the networks worked, the data speed was found to be unreliable or slow - stuck under 15 Mbps. This meant that many people in the heart of the West End would struggle with basic tasks, such as loading maps or making video calls.
However, tests on the same streets at less busy times found that all four networks performed well, highlighting an issue of congestion rather than coverage.
Struggling for a signal in London Bridge
Adikalie Sumah, from Southwark, runs a shoe cleaning business CureCleans and recently relocated to a new office near London bridge.
The move was designed to create easier access for customers and delivery drivers to drop off and collect their shoes, but he says the mobile signal is so bad he struggles to take calls inside the office.
He uses EE, but the rest of the team use a range of network providers including O2 and Three.
Adikalie said: "When we're trying to contact customers to pick up and drop off their shoe, it's a bit of a struggle trying to get through to them."
'I take calls outside'
Like any business, they take a lot of phone calls for scheduling shifts, making orders and organising deliveries but the poor service makes this difficult.
At the moment, he manages this problem by taking phone calls outside the office and leaves all the doors and windows open to improve the signal but said this has meant they sometimes get complaints from the neighbours.
He added that with winter approaching and the noise complaints taking calls outside the office would no longer be an option.
He contacted his landlord about the issue but was told nothing could be done to improve it.
Adikalie mainly subcontracts young people across Southwark helping them to gain work experience.
He hopes to keep offering these opportunities but worries poor mobile service could hold the company back.
![A man wearing a knitted cap and grey hoodie with a white  t-shirt underneath. In the background there are multiple monitors and a PS5 console on the desk.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/1a2e/live/82d297a0-b0d8-11f1-b427-b9b4ddc559ae.jpg)
Joshua Folorunsho struggles to find mobile service in central London
Joshua Folorunsho, 22, from Peckham is a full-time content creator and employee at CureCleans.
He is known as JTA across his social media platforms and creates content for the company.
"Obviously this is my livelihood so without it I'm not able to eat and put clothes on my back, so it's very important to me."
Joshua has been with Three since he was 15 but said: "Sometimes when I call people it doesn't even ring, but I have service."
He said he struggles to find a reliable mobile signal when travelling across central London unless he's "lucky".
Joshua said he contacted a Three store in his local area but was told there was nothing they could do, and that they also had poor mobile service.
'I'm losing pay'
Victoria Olaofe, 24, from Bermondsey works as a sales representative near St Pauls, and her poor mobile service means that she misses out on pay.
"There have been occasions where my manager has tried to contact me, but I simply haven't received the calls or messages until much later. It's even affected things like clocking in on my phone."
Victoria gets paid by the hour and needs to clock into work using her phone, but her mobile data becomes unusable once she's in central London. This means she cannot clock in until hours later.
She said there does not seem to be any solution so she just loses pay.
"I've also tried troubleshooting the issue. My mum even contacted Three after experiencing poor coverage in her area, and although my experience isn't identical to hers, it made me realise there may be a wider issue."
In response to a social media call out, Victoria said: "I realised I'm clearly not the only person experiencing this.
"It was reassuring to see that others are reporting similar issues, although it's concerning that so many people seem to be affected."
What action is being taken?
Experts say capacity shortfalls during busy times, housing development and planning regulations are partly to blame, with rules varying across London's 33 councils - creating more challenges for network providers.
A spokesperson for London Councils, which represents all the local authorities in the capital, said: "The London Growth Plan and London Infrastructure Framework we developed jointly with the mayor highlight the importance of digital infrastructure and mobile connectivity.
"There is a range of factors behind the current connectivity problems, but boroughs take this issue seriously and are working with network providers and other partners to help resolve them," they added.
Mobile UK has said that mobile operators have invested "billions of pounds to upgrade their networks across London" and are committed to working with the government and local councils to improve mobile phone service.
The organisation also said it recognised that the Draft London Plan, external acknowledged the challenge of housing development for mobile operators in London but it wants urgent policy reform on planning and a "unified framework that treats digital infrastructure as a priority".
The Department for Culture, Media and Sport has been asked for comment.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: Mobile phone reception and internet speeds in London have deteriorated, with global rankings falling and over a third of UK customers reporting poor signal issues. The problems are driven by a combination of network congestion during peak hours and the loss of antenna sites due to new building developments. This lack of connectivity is negatively impacting Londoners' livelihoods, businesses, and ability to perform daily tasks.
key_points: London recently fell to 91st place in global internet speed rankings.
New property developments often force mobile operators to remove antennas, leaving coverage gaps because finding replacement sites takes longer than the provided notice period.
Areas like Covent Garden and Liverpool Street suffer from severe network congestion during peak rush hours, causing data tests to fail despite users having full signal bars.
Poor mobile service is harming local businesses and workers, resulting in missed calls, difficulties scheduling deliveries, and delayed work clock-ins that affect pay.
Network providers are calling for urgent planning policy reforms and a unified framework across London's local authorities to prioritize digital infrastructure.

title: It’s official: London is home to the best pizza restaurant in the world
author: Roisin Teeling
content:
[title]
Step aside, Naples. Move over, New York. If you want the best slice of pizza on the planet, you only need to jump on the District line to Chiswick.
London’s own Napoli on the Road has just been named the World’s Best Pizzeria at the 50 Top Pizza World Awards. Founded by chef Michele Pascarella, the restaurant celebrated the win at a ceremony at Teatro Mercadante in Naples – the perfect place to pull off a victory like this. If you are going to be named the best ’za on earth, you might as well do it in the city that invented it.
