![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
US officials secretly flew an American diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children out of the UK without telling British police, it has been reported.
American personnel have no powers of arrest in Britain and, The Sun reported, there was no formal request for the man to be extradited.
UK ministers are understood to be in contact with the US embassy over the incident, which could further strain relations between London and Washington.
“As a US investigation is ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage.”
The man’s seizure is reported to be related to an investigation into another individual in the US.
A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said: “On Tuesday August 25, US authorities made us aware of an investigation they are conducting into suspected offences in London relating to indecent images of children.
“We continue to liaise with them regarding this matter.”
The incident comes two months after then-deputy prime minister David Lammy said he would raise with the US government the case of an American fighter pilot who avoided a trial under English law for strangling a woman in Cambridge.
Captain Jacob Wulfson was tried at a court martial on a US airbase, despite his alleged crime taking place while he was off-duty, and was jailed for six months after being convicted of strangulation.
He was acquitted of charges of sexual assault and aggravated sexual contact.
Downing Street said at the time it was “very concerning” that Capt Wulfson’s case had not been dealt with by the Crown Prosecution Service.
A US embassy spokesperson said: “We are aware of allegations concerning an individual assigned to the US Embassy in London. The United States government expects all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct, and we take these allegations seriously.
“While we can’t comment on the specifics of the case, we quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action, and we will continue to work closely with our law enforcement partners regarding these allegations.
“The individual in question has been reassigned to the United States in conjunction with an ongoing investigation. The Embassy has informed British authorities of the case.”
summary: US officials secretly flew an American diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children out of the UK without informing British police or making a formal extradition request. UK ministers are in contact with the US embassy regarding the incident, which follows previous diplomatic tensions over US personnel avoiding British legal proceedings. The US embassy stated that the individual has been reassigned to the United States in conjunction with an ongoing investigation and that British authorities were informed.
key_points: An American diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children was flown out of the UK by US officials.
The departure occurred without notifying British police or making a formal extradition request.
UK ministers are in contact with the US embassy over the incident, which may strain bilateral relations.
The US embassy stated that the individual was reassigned to the US as part of an ongoing investigation.

title: TfL moves step closer to bringing London buses into public ownership
author: Kumail Jaffer
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![London: The bus driver brightening daily life with a bubble gun](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/06/27/11/33/2356363-library.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Officials are set to start engaging bus operators later this month to discuss the feasibility of bringing currently franchised services in house, according to sources familiar with the talks. The proposals were first laid out earlier this year in TfL’s business plan, where officials said that as part of a move to “reimagine London’s bus network, we will develop detailed proposals for a new publicly owned bus company for London.” The study will “assess how this could further support innovation, efficiencies and accountability, and support the needs of customers and the workforce.” Under the current model, private firms submit bids to TfL to run franchised services, with contracts generally running for seven years and setting performance targets for bus operators with a set income. ![

Sadiq Khan has vowed to do more to help bus drivers suffering in the heat on London buses

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/06/27/11/33/2356363-library.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) There are 16 privately-owned operators on the capital’s 675 bus routes, including Arriva, Go-Ahead London, First Bus London, and Stage Coach London. Should a publicly owned company be launched, when franchise contracts come to an end, TfL could bring them under the new public bus operator. Such a move would fulfil a promise made by the Mayor of London in his 2024 election manifesto. In August that year, Sir Sadiq Khan told the London Assembly that there were “lots of upsides in us having a publicly owned bus company”, including being able to reinvest any profit back into public transport infrastructure. TfL are now able to do so thanks to the Bus Services Act passed by the Labour government last year, which lifted the ban on local authorities setting up their own bus companies. Read More “This will stop money flowing from Londoners and Transport for London to private companies who preside over a race to the bottom culture that impacts drivers and services.” She told the LDRS: “Bringing some bus operations directly into public ownership could give TfL greater control over how services are run, improve reliability and safety, and mean money made from operating services can be reinvested in London’s transport network. ![

London buses

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/14/9/42/GettyImages-2276201750.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) “If TfL is now taking practical steps towards establishing a publicly owned bus operator, I very much welcome that progress. I’ve been making the case for TfL to explore this option for some time and I want to see it developed into a serious part of the plan for improving London’s buses.” Festus Akinbusoye, who is running to be Conservative Candidate for Mayor of London, suggested such a move was unnecessary, however. “Londoners want reliable, affordable buses; they don’t care who owns the company operating them. Sadiq Khan is trying to fix a problem that simply isn’t there. London’s bus franchising model works. “Other cities in the UK and internationally aim to replicate the success of London. “Rather than spending taxpayers’ money and years of effort setting up a publicly owned operator, we should be asking how that successful model can be replicated elsewhere in the country. “All that bringing bus operations in-house achieves is higher costs and more bureaucracy, not better services. “As Mayor, I would protect what works. TfL should focus its time and taxpayers’ money on improving services, tackling fare evasion and making journeys better for Londoners – not dismantling a successful model to win a round of applause from Labour activists.” Last week, Reform Assembly Member Keith Prince told a fringe event at the party’s annual conference in Birmingham that the rest of the UK would do well to learn from London’s franchising system. A TfL spokesperson said: “As part of our work to reimagine London’s bus network, we are currently developing detailed proposals for a new publicly owned bus company for London. “We are assessing how this could further support innovation, efficiencies and accountability, and support the needs of customers and the workforce.”
summary: Transport for London (TfL) is preparing to engage bus operators to discuss the feasibility of establishing a publicly owned bus company. The proposals follow TfL's business plan and fulfill a commitment made by the Mayor of London in his 2024 election manifesto. While supporters argue the move will improve reliability and reinvest profits into infrastructure, critics contend that the current franchising model already works well and that public ownership will only increase costs and bureaucracy.
key_points: TfL is beginning discussions with bus operators to evaluate bringing franchised services in-house.
Currently, 16 private operators run London's 675 bus routes under seven-year franchise contracts.
The initiative fulfills a 2024 election manifesto promise by the Mayor of London and is enabled by the recent Bus Services Act.
Supporters claim public ownership will improve safety, reliability, and allow profits to be reinvested, whereas critics argue it creates unnecessary bureaucracy and higher costs.

title: The London children trapped in Britain’s £500m County Lines drug trade
author: Hannah Wallace
content:
![The London children trapped in Britain’s £500m County Lines drug trade](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/9/56/county-lines-investigation.jpeg?trim=0,39,0,39&quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
At 14, Casper* should have been sitting in a classroom. Instead, he was trafficked out of London to help transport and sell heroin and crack cocaine. For weeks, he was held inside a filthy “trap house” — a property transformed into a drug gang operating base. During multiple moves to new locations, gang members ordered him to hide Class
A drugs inside his body — likely his anus — to evade police detection. Beatings became routine as Casper’s captors enforced obedience through fear. They targeted his family as well, repeatedly vandalising their London home. If Casper tried to leave, they put a gun to his head.
The Youth Endowment Fund estimates that one in eight British children aged 13 to 17 has been approached to sell or transport drugs
Nearly two decades after London’s postcode gangs began expanding beyond the capital, county lines has evolved into one of Britain’s most profitable criminal enterprises, generating up to £500 million a year supplying crack cocaine and heroin across England and Wales, according to National Crime Agency data.
What began as gangs exporting drugs to coastal and market towns has become a sophisticated countrywide network of child criminal exploitation, “cuckooed” homes, money laundering and manufactured debt bondage. The foundation of this corporate-style hierarchy is children — some as young as 11 — who are used to transport drugs, cash and weapons.
The Youth Endowment Fund estimates that one in eight British children aged 13 to 17 has been approached to sell or transport drugs. In London alone, more than 4,000 children have reportedly been groomed or coerced into county lines operations, according to official city data.
Children might be groomed with nothing more than a bucket of fried chicken
Child exploitation often begins with grooming. Caseworkers and frontline specialists told the Standard they repeatedly see the same pattern: fractured, low-income families rife with abuse, neglect, and children with unmet special educational needs, such as ADHD or autism.
Gang members exploit financial hardship and social isolation by offering what appears to be friendship, belonging and status. The rewards start small: a bit of cash, then maybe designer trainers or clothing. On some of London’s poorest estates, youth workers say children might be groomed with nothing more than a bucket of fried chicken. Need and naivety make them particularly vulnerable.
“Children are often deliberately targeted because they are children,” says Junior Smart, associate director at the St Giles Trust. “They can be easier to impress, frighten, isolate or control, and they are less likely to understand that what is being presented as friendship, money, protection or status is actually exploitation.”
Once dependency is established, the grooming escalates. Many children are put through violent initiations, from carrying weapons and assaulting rivals to setting up drug lines in new towns — missions that frequently place them directly in conflict with competing gangs. In one case, gang members reportedly forced a 14-year-old boy to rape a girl as part of his initiation. Casper’s story exposes repeated failures on the part of institutions created to protect vulnerable children like him. He grew up with a single mother on an estate known for gang activity. Money was tight.
His mother worked long hours, often leaving him unsupervised. Excluded from school at 12, Casper spent extended periods missing from education. Despite the clear warning signs, nobody contacted social services — a critical missed opportunity.
Read More
Ewan’s* childhood followed a familiar pattern. Referred to the St Giles Trust aged 16 in 2025, he had already experienced years of trauma, missing episodes, criminal exploitation and deteriorating mental health. Known to services from the age of six after growing up in a chaotic home, Ewan’s childhood was marked by trauma and missed opportunities for support. He began using cannabis at just 10, trying to cope with experiences that had left him struggling. By 12, he had been drawn into county lines exploitation to fund his drug use. Within a year, his cannabis use had escalated to as much as six grams a day, while concerns grew over possible gang involvement and he began repeatedly going missing.
Exclusion removes a much-needed protective environment, creating a vacuum gangs are quick to fill
Analysts increasingly view school exclusion as a key risk factor for criminal exploitation, as it cuts young people off from the support and stability schools often provide. “The vast majority of the children — and many of the adults — we work with have histories of school exclusion or persistent absence,” says Dr Grace Robinson, founder of Black Box Research and Consultancy, which specialises in countering modern slavery and criminal exploitation. “School is often one of the last remaining protective structures in a child’s life. It provides routine, trusted adults, positive peer relationships and opportunities for professionals to identify indicators of exploitation.”
When a young person is outside the schooling system, isolated from helpful adults, or feels labelled and unwanted, that creates space for exploiters to step in. Exclusion removes a much-needed protective environment, creating a vacuum gangs are quick to fill. Ironically, many of the behaviours that trigger exclusion — truancy, drug possession or carrying weapons — are themselves some of the strongest indicators that a child may already be exploited.
Robinson says some schools have responded to behavioural incidents by calling police to remove pupils from the premises. “Such a response can be profoundly distressing and may reinforce feelings of rejection and criminalisation, further weakening the child’s trust in professionals and making engagement with safeguarding support less likely,” she says.
Many excluded pupils are then transferred into Pupil Referral Units, becoming concentrated in environments gangs regularly target. These schools operate under reduced timetables, which means young people with working parents are often left unsupervised.
Practitioners say support often focused on managing the consequences rather than addressing the causes of his vulnerability
Ewan’s education followed the same trajectory. He was excluded from three mainstream schools before being placed in alternative provision, but struggled to attend and eventually left education at 15 without any qualifications. Diagnosed as autistic, he also experienced severe mental health difficulties and twice attempted to take his own life. By then, multiple agencies had already been involved in his life. His exclusions, mental health crises and repeated contact with authorities had provided opportunities for intervention, but practitioners say support often focused on managing the consequences rather than addressing the causes of his vulnerability.
Even when social services intervene, the response is often undermined by years of financial pressure. Children are frequently placed in care homes or temporary accommodation far outside London. These out-of-area placements are widely portrayed as helping break gang connections, but practitioners say they are often a result of limited local placements and stretched council budgets.
Casper’s arrest exposed perhaps the most serious institutional failure of all. Police found him almost 100 miles from home. He had fallen way behind on his education while living in a trap house selling Class A drugs. Yet the authorities failed to place him into the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), the government framework for identifying victims of modern slavery and human trafficking.
Under the Modern Slavery Act, police and other public authorities have a statutory duty to refer children into NRM whenever there are reasonable grounds to suspect exploitation. The threshold is deliberately low, and placing a child into NRM is merely a recognition that he or she may have been trafficked and compelled to commit crimes. But lawyers and frontline practitioners say too many exploited children are still viewed primarily as offenders. Children groomed into county lines are frequently traumatised, distrustful of authority and reluctant to cooperate with police.
Yet investigators often interpret inconsistent accounts, silence or repeated returns to gangs as evidence of criminal intent rather than signs of coercive control. “We have seen a number of cases where police have been asked by defence solicitors to act as first responders and refer a potential child victim into the NRM but have refused because they did not believe there were reasonable grounds to suspect modern slavery, despite credible indicators,” says Robinson.
Even when a child is recognised by the NRM, state protections only go so far. Schools could still treat that child as a disciplinary problem, the police as a missing person, the criminal justice system as a defendant. Crucially, NRM decisions are not binding on prosecutors and cannot be relied on as evidence in criminal proceedings.
Defence solicitors say this creates a postcode lottery of justice, where whether an exploited child is recognised as a victim or prosecuted as a criminal can come down to discretion, or location.
Yet practitioners say recognising exploitation is only the first step. Helping a child leave county lines often requires months of patient, trauma-informed support built on trust rather than punishment. That was the approach taken when Ewan was referred to St Giles after years of criminal exploitation. Agencies warned a caseworker that Ewan did not engage with professionals. Instead of overwhelming him with targets, staff at St Giles adapted their approach around Ewan’s autism, trauma and mental health needs, focusing on building trust.
The children most easily labelled as criminals are often those the state has failed for the longest
If London and Britain are serious about ending county lines, policing alone will not solve a crisis rooted in poverty, exclusion and eroded public services. The Metropolitan Police continues to shut down hundreds of drug lines every month. But enforcement addresses the symptoms, not the causes. School absence remains poorly monitored, youth services have been hollowed out and councils continue to struggle under financial pressure. Recent legislation, including the Crime and Policing Act, has strengthened offences relating to child criminal exploitation. Yet some worry about creating more offences to address modern slavery when police are inadequately trained to identify such cases.
Robinson says few cases have led to what might be described as a thorough investigation. The children most easily labelled as criminals are often those the state has failed for the longest. Experts argue the answer lies in identifying exploitation much earlier: intervening before children disappear from school, improving information-sharing between agencies, rebuilding support services and ensuring safeguarding responses take precedence over criminalisation.
Until that changes, children like Casper will continue to be treated as criminals.
*Names have been changed
summary: County lines has evolved into a £500 million criminal enterprise in Britain, heavily reliant on the exploitation and grooming of vulnerable children from low-income or fractured families. Children as young as 11 are coerced into transporting drugs and cash, frequently facing severe violence, debt bondage, and institutional failures. Experts emphasize that tackling the crisis requires addressing root causes such as poverty, school exclusions, and a lack of early safeguarding interventions, rather than relying solely on criminal enforcement.
key_points: The Youth Endowment Fund estimates that one in eight British children aged 13 to 17 has been approached to sell or transport drugs.
County lines generates up to £500 million a year supplying crack cocaine and heroin across England and Wales.
Grooming often targets children dealing with poverty, neglect, or unmet special educational needs by offering false friendship, cash, or status.
School exclusions act as a major risk factor by removing protective environments and creating vacuums that gangs quickly fill.
Vulnerable children are frequently treated as criminal offenders rather than victims of modern slavery due to institutional failures and a lack of proper referrals.

title: A north London bar is launching a Guinness afternoon tea
author: India Lawrence
content:
[title]
Thought we were firmly past the Guinness craze? Think again. Because in what we’re calling the biggest crossover between straight male DJs and middle-aged mums since, well... ever, one bar in north London has decided to launch a Guinness afternoon tea.
Homeboy on Essex Road is launching the Guinness-themed tea from October this year. It makes sense, given that Homeboy is an Irish cocktail bar.
For this afternoon treat Homeboy going both sweet and savoury. Guests will be able to munch on Irish smoked salmon on Guinness soda bread, a beef and Guinness stew and an Irish beef slider with Guinness gravy. For sweet, the menu includes Guinness cake and a black velvet blancmange.
Bookings include a welcome drink, and guests can choose from a pint of the black stuff, frozen Irish coffee with Guinness infusion, or a pot of Barry’s tea. There’s also an option for a drinks pairing, which allows diners to order a black velvet (Guinness and champagne) or a baby Guinness.
Guinness afternoon tea at Homeboy begins on October 10 and can be booked online. The normal afternoon tea is £45 and with the drinks pairing it’s £65. With Homeboy’s expertly made cocktails and convivial Irish pub atmosphere, we expect this stout-y afternoon tea could be a real winner.
Did you see that a massive new bar will open inside London’s iconic Admiralty Arch?
Get the latest and greatest from the Big Smoke – from news and reviews to events and trends. Just follow our Time Out London WhatsApp channel.
Stay in the loop: sign up to our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
summary: Homeboy, an Irish cocktail bar on Essex Road in north London, is launching a Guinness-themed afternoon tea starting October 10. The menu features both sweet and savoury items incorporating Guinness, alongside a welcome drink of choice. Pricing is set at £45 for the normal afternoon tea or £65 with a drinks pairing.
key_points: Homeboy bar on Essex Road is launching a Guinness-themed afternoon tea.
The menu includes Guinness-infused items like Irish smoked salmon on soda bread, beef stew, a beef slider, cake, and blancmange.
Bookings include a welcome drink such as a pint of Guinness, frozen Irish coffee with Guinness, or Barry's tea.
The afternoon tea begins on October 10 and costs £45, or £65 with a drinks pairing.

title: Labour launches campaign in crunch London by-election against the Green Party
author: Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/12/13/18/holborn-by-election.jpg?trim=28,0,47,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali has pledged to give children the “best possible start in life” as she launches her campaign for the upcoming by-election.
Ms Abdi-Wali said she wants families across the constituency to have the same “security and opportunity” she was afforded after arriving in the UK as a child refugee in the early 1990s, fleeing the civil war in Somalia.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/12/13/30/labour-launch.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The Holborn and St Pancras by-election is scheduled to take place on October 8 following Sir Keir’s departure from front-line politics to focus on a role in international affairs.
If elected, Ms Abdi-Wali would become the first British-Somali woman to serve as an MP in the UK.
Joined by local MPs Georgia Gould and Florence Eshalomi at her campaign launch on Saturday, Ms Abdi-Wali promised to keep housing at the heart of her campaign, pointing to her record of investment in and improvements to Camden’s council homes.
She also pledged to continue putting families and children first.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/12/13/10/labour-launch-1.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
In local government, she backed Camden’s Pregnancy Grant for eligible parents and the rollout of free breakfasts for children across the borough, with ten local schools already benefiting from the scheme
She also highlighted tackling homelessness as a priority – an issue shared with Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
“Camden gave my family a home, hope, and opportunity when we needed it most. I’ve never forgotten that, and I’ve spent my life working to give that same hope back to the community,” Ms Abdi-Wali said.
“I want every child growing up here and every family who calls this place home to have that same security and opportunity.
Read More
“That means more homes people can afford, giving families the support they need and making sure every child gets the best possible start in life.
“I’m proud of what we’ve delivered together in Camden, but I know there is so much more to do. Labour’s campaign is about bringing our community together to make hope win in Holborn and St Pancras.”
Housing is also emerging as a key battleground in the contest, with Mr Polanski putting affordable homes and rent controls at the forefront of the Green campaign.
Commenting on his selection as the Green Party candidate, Mr Polanski said: “I love this place and so do the people whose doors I’ve knocked on in recent days – but it can be even better. I know times are tough in Holborn and St Pancras.
“My story of constant moving around flats is such a common story for Londoners – and I know many people here are really struggling right now. I’ll fight to turn this around.
“Greens are underdogs here but we have the momentum – and I know we can achieve a historic victory in one of Labour’s safest seats.
“We will fight a positive campaign on the issues we know people care about, and to put as much pressure as we can on Labour to lower bills, for much more affordable housing and rent controls, to reduce massive wealth inequality and to make sure Labour don’t back down on climate action by allowing more North Sea drilling.
“If elected, I will fight every day, in this constituency and in the Houses of Parliament, for the things people care about. Against injustice and on the side of ordinary people, not big money and the powerful.”
summary: Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali has launched her campaign for the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, pledging to focus on housing, families, and giving children the best start in life. The by-election is scheduled for October 8 following Sir Keir's departure, and if elected, Ms Abdi-Wali would become the first British-Somali woman to serve as an MP. Meanwhile, Green Party candidate Mr Polanski is campaigning on issues including affordable housing, rent controls, lowering bills, and climate action.
key_points: Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali launched her campaign for the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.
The by-election is set for October 8 following Sir Keir's departure from front-line politics.
Ms Abdi-Wali would become the first British-Somali woman to serve as an MP if elected.
Housing, affordable homes, and support for families are central battlegrounds in the contest against Green Party candidate Mr Polanski.

title: Thousands of e-bikes seized in the last year as anger grows over dockless bikes
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after poorly parked cycles force blind man into busy road](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/02/10/16/10162558-f42cebde-c9e0-4598-8353-a389d5ef09d9.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Local authorities across the city have seized 3,393 dangerously parked or abandoned ebikes so far this year, according to an investigation by The Guardian - a 23% increase from the whole of 2025. Lime bikes accounted for more than 2,000 of the seizures this year, according to data that was provided by 19 reporting authorities under a Freedom of Information request. Forest ranked second, with 978 seizures, followed by Voi at 103. Dockless ebikes have surged in popularity in recent years, being used for one in 10 of the 1.5m daily cycle journeys in the city, according to estimates by TfL. Erik Matthies, policy lead at the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB), said that the rise in abandoned bikes was “overwhelming” blind and partially sighted people, as well as elderly people and wheelchair users. Mr Matthies told the Guardian: “People are having collisions and injuries due to bikes left on the pavement, and the problem is getting worse. “There are blind people who tell us they do not go out on their own any more and they do not make journeys that they used to.” Zak Viney, from campaign group Living Streets, added: “Irresponsibly parked ebikes cause a lot of problems. It prevents people from walking and wheeling on the street safely.” ![

A Voi E-bike in Ealing

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/08/18/51/Voi-e-bike.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) James Slater, a councillor in Camden, said: “We need to have a London-wide approach. It’s very difficult for 32 councils in London to all have slightly different policies, and in some cases different operators on borough boundaries.” However, the bike operators have argued that councils are not investing sufficiently in building more parking bays, which could prevent such build-ups. Read More A spokesperson for Lime said: “The vast majority of our riders end their trips responsibly, and a very small proportion of total rides result in seizures and fines by councils. “We recognise that parking is a challenge across the industry largely due to ebike parking not keeping pace with growing demand for rental ebike services.” The mayor of London’s office said it was working closely with TfL and the DfT to implement “much-needed controls as quickly as possible”. A spokesperson said: “It’s vital that safety improvements sit at the heart of any future regulation to ensure the industry can continue to thrive. “The mayor continues to urge all dockless operators to fully engage with London boroughs and TfL to ensure their services work well for all Londoners.”
summary: Local authorities in London have seized 3,393 dangerously parked or abandoned e-bikes so far this year, marking a 23% increase from the previous year. Campaigners and disability advocates warn that the incorrectly parked bikes are creating dangerous hazards for blind, elderly, and disabled pedestrians. While operators argue that councils have failed to build enough parking infrastructure to keep up with demand, local officials are calling for a unified, London-wide approach to regulate the industry.
key_points: Local authorities seized 3,393 abandoned or dangerously parked e-bikes, with Lime accounting for over 2,000 of them.
Advocacy groups report that poorly parked bikes are causing injuries and forcing some blind and elderly residents to stay home.
Operators state that parking infrastructure has failed to keep pace with the growing demand for rental e-bikes.
Local councillors are calling for a standardized, London-wide regulatory approach instead of fragmented borough policies.

title: Southern trains to be reduced near Lewes to help protect tracks
author: Daniel Sexton
content:
![A green Southern train arrives at Hastings station](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/a760/live/48b0e1a0-ae7e-11f1-ab4e-59a2f08e4172.jpg)
No direct trains will run between between Eastbourne/Ore and London Victoria during off-peak hours
- Published
Trains on a main rail route between the East Sussex coast and London will not run in off-peak hours for four weeks after track conditions were affected by the hot and dry weather over summer.
Southern Rail says that no trains will run directly between Eastbourne/Ore and London Victoria, via Lewes and Haywards Heath, between 09:00 BST and 16:15 on Mondays through to Friday.
Services from Eastbourne will run hourly to and from Haywards Heath, where passengers can change for onward connections to the capital, as well as Gatwick Airport.
One train will also operate hourly between Ore and Eastbourne in both directions.
Passengers have been told to allow more time for their journeys, although those travelling from Ore, Hastings and St Leonards Warrior Square can use Southeastern services at no extra cost.
The operator said that no trains in peak hours are affected, and while it apologised for the disruption, it added that the "temporary timetable will help provide a more reliable service and reduce last-minute changes".
The temporary timetable starts on Monday.
![Undated handout photo issued by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) of the aerial view of the site of the derailment of a passenger train at Lewes.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/958/cpsprodpb/7596/live/9852c6b0-ae7e-11f1-ab4e-59a2f08e4172.jpg)
The stretch of track between Lewes and Haywards Heath was closed for 19 days after a derailment
Part of the route where trains have been reduced was the scene of a train derailment in August 2026.
Coaches on a train from London to Eastbourne tumbled down an embankment close to Lewes, leaving 30 people injured, two of those seriously.
An investigation by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch said that a track defect was reported close to the site of the derailment.
The stretch of track was closed for 19 days to allow an investigation to take place and for repairs to be made, before it reopened on 1 September.
Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk , external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: Southern Rail is reducing off-peak train services on the route between the East Sussex coast and London Victoria for four weeks due to track conditions affected by summer weather. Direct trains will not run between 09:00 and 16:15 on weekdays, requiring passengers to change at Haywards Heath. The temporary timetable follows a passenger train derailment near Lewes in August 2026 caused by a track defect.
key_points: No direct off-peak trains will run between Eastbourne/Ore and London Victoria from Monday through Friday.
Services from Eastbourne will run hourly to Haywards Heath for passengers to connect to London and Gatwick Airport.
Peak hour services are not affected by the temporary four-week timetable.
The adjustments follow an August 2026 derailment near Lewes that injured 30 people and led to a 19-day track closure.

title: Traders face £800 fines in crackdown on al-fresco dining London hotspot
author: Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
A popular London al-fresco dining hotspot that sprang up during Covid is under threat as traders face being slapped with £800 fines if they do not move their outdoor seating, it has been revealed.
The market, which features around 32 stalls, developed its al-fresco dining culture during the Covid pandemic, when emergency measures allowed businesses across the country to serve customers outside and helped many stay afloat.
Business owners say the arrangement at Exmouth Market has continued under a ‘gentleman’s agreement’ in the six years since.
But traders now fear the future of the popular dining spot is at risk after Islington Council issued a directive requiring them to remove large portions of their outside tables and chairs or face £800 fines.
To comply with updated pavement licensing rules, restaurants and bars are being told to reduce their outdoor seating capacity by an estimated 40 per cent, according to traders.
They will also be required to create a two-metre gap between their tables and the pavement, up from the current 0.8 metres.
Gareth Kerr, who runs Cafe Kick, a bar on the street, told The Times: “To take away 40 per cent of your trade overnight or with only a two-week grace period puts many of these small businesses in real danger of insolvency.
“Instead of starting with enforcement the council should start with dialogue.
“This isn’t McDonald’s.”
Mr Kerr has called on council officers, police and other stakeholders to meet with traders and draw up a potential roadmap for the area.
Read More
The Exmouth Market Traders Association, which includes many of the bars and restaurants on the road, agrees there could be changes and compromises.
But its members object to the suddenness of the threat and what they say is a lack of dialogue.
In August, traders adhered to the council’s tighter restrictions for the evenings, which they claim resulted in the market becoming like a ‘ghost town’.
The council applied for pedestrianisation under the GLA’s Summer Streets scheme this year — a City Hall-led scheme providing funding for temporary al fresco schemes — but was rejected.
The council told local newspaper the Islington Tribune, which first reported the crackdown: “We have not taken any formal enforcement action in relation to tables and chairs licensing at Exmouth Market.
“Those wishing to trade with tables and chairs outside are free to apply for a licence and several businesses have done so in recent weeks.
“We will continue to work with traders to support understanding and compliance, while taking a fair and consistent approach for businesses, residents and other users of the street.”
Islington Council has been approached by The Standard for comment.
summary: Traders at London's Exmouth Market face £800 fines and threats to their businesses after Islington Council ordered them to remove large portions of their outdoor seating. The directive requires businesses to cut outdoor seating capacity by about 40 per cent and leave a two-metre gap on the pavement to comply with updated licensing rules. While traders object to the sudden enforcement and lack of dialogue, the council stated it has not taken formal enforcement action and encourages businesses to apply for licenses.
key_points: Traders at Exmouth Market face £800 fines if they fail to remove large portions of their outdoor seating.
Businesses are being asked to reduce outdoor seating capacity by 40 per cent and maintain a two-metre gap on the pavement.
Traders argue the sudden crackdown and tight two-week grace period threaten their businesses with insolvency.
The Exmouth Market Traders Association objects to the lack of dialogue from the council regarding the changes.
Islington Council stated it has not taken formal enforcement action and encourages businesses to apply for proper licenses.

title: A decade of London’s bus hopper fare
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
A decade of London’s bus hopper fare
London’s Hopper bus fare turns ten this weekend, having been used for more than 1.4 billion free bus and tram changes since its introduction.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/TfL-Image-Mayor-Sadiq-Khan-at-the-launch-of-the-Hopper-Fare-in-September-2026.jpg)
Launched on 12th September 2016, the fare lets passengers paying by Oyster or contactless make additional bus and tram journeys without paying again, provided they touch in within an hour of their first journey.
The original version permitted one free transfer. It was expanded in January 2018 to allow unlimited bus and tram journeys within the hour. More than 100 million free changes were made during its first year, and the total has since passed 1.43 billion.
However, the anniversary comes as TfL continues to reduce parts of the bus network, either by cutting routes or reducing service frequency to cope with slower traffic speeds.
Forty routes had their frequencies reduced between April 2024 and March 2026, according to figures provided to the London Assembly, although TfL said it also increased frequencies on 71 routes during the same period. TfL says it continues to tackle pinch-points along bus routes through junction improvements and technological upgrades at traffic signal junctions, with 500 bus-priority traffic signal timing reviews underway and 135 traffic signal schemes to be delivered across London by the end of March 2027.
Paradoxically, the cuts make the Hopper Fare more useful as it helps when direct services are changed to require changing buses.
This summer, City Hall temporarily extended the Hopper principle at weekends, allowing unlimited bus and tram travel for £1.75 on Saturdays, Sundays and the August bank holiday. TfL says 6.8 million passengers used the offer during its eight-week run, collectively saving an estimated £15 million.
Sadiq Khan said the permanent Hopper fare had made bus travel “simpler, more affordable and fairer”, particularly for passengers whose journeys require a change.
London’s buses remain the capital’s most heavily used form of public transport, carrying more than five million passengers on a typical day. TfL says 96 per cent of households are within 400 metres of a bus stop. The network is also being reshaped through the expansion of the Superloop express routes in outer London, including the recently opened SL12 between Gants Hill and Rainham.
Buses also play a crucial role in reducing road congestion, carrying up to 80 times as many passengers as a car while using only around three times as much road space.
summary: London's Hopper bus fare is celebrating its tenth anniversary, having facilitated over 1.4 billion free bus and tram transfers since its launch in September 2016. The scheme initially offered one free transfer and was later expanded to allow unlimited journeys within an hour for passengers using Oyster or contactless payment. While the anniversary coincides with TfL implementing some route cuts and service reductions to address slower traffic speeds, the Hopper fare remains vital as a way to offset the need for multiple tickets when changing buses.
key_points: London's Hopper bus fare turns ten after being introduced on 12th September 2016.
The scheme has been used for more than 1.43 billion free bus and tram changes.
Passengers using Oyster or contactless can make unlimited journeys within an hour of their first touch-in.
A summer weekend trial of the Hopper principle allowed unlimited travel for £1.75, saving passengers an estimated £15 million.
London buses carry more than five million passengers on a typical day and remain the capital's most heavily used public transport.

title: What it's really like for young London renters
author: Prudence Ivey
content:
![Londoners share what it really takes to survive renting in the capital](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/9/30/Withnail-I.jpeg?width=1600&auto=webp&quality=75) Flat broke: What it's really like for young London renters As graduates head to the capital to start their careers, Prudence Ivey looks at whether even the dingiest flatshare is affordable in 2026 ![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Can you truly claim to be a Londoner if you didn’t spend your early adulthood in the capital living in grotty digs with an evolving cast of oddballs and dishwashing shirkers? Immortalised in everything from The Young Ones to This Life, Spaced, Peep Show and Crashing, it’s a lifestyle approved by none other than Margot Robbie, who often speaks of her time in a Clapham house share as one of the happiest in her life. At best this scenario fixed you up with a crowd of like-minded friends for life. At worst, you would line up a series of hilarious anecdotes to make you seem edgy during a staid middle age. ![

NEW YORK, NEW YORK - MAY 04: Margot Robbie attends the Saint Laurent Met Gala after party at People's Bar on May 04, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Ilya S. Savenok/Getty Images for Saint Laurent)

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/05/05/11/2274596482.jpg?trim=282,0,2744,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) But is any of this horror and hilarity even an option for today’s graduates and first-jobbers, even those lucky ones with a wage? There has always been a financial motivation for living in “bohemian” squalor, but rents have risen steadily in a way that starter salaries have not, putting even the crummiest rooms out of bounds for some. The average cost of renting a room in inner London currently stands at £979 per month, according to flatshare site SpareRoom. To be classed as “affordable”, housing should take up no more than 30 per cent of your take-home pay, but as many as 40 per cent of London renters now shell out more than half of their incomes on rent. And that’s if they can even find a room. Rental supply has dwindled in the capital thanks to increased taxes on landlords and now the Renters’ Rights Act, which came into force earlier this year and precipitated a five per cent drop in flat share supply. “Graduates entering the post-summer rent rush will find competition in London is high,” says Matt Hutchinson, communications director of SpareRoom. “Rental supply in the capital is now in decline and, because of the high cost of living, graduates are battling for rooms in flatshares with a growing number of young and middle-aged workers who’ve been priced out of renting solo or buying.” ![Fresh Meat Series 4 Channel 4/Ray Burmiston](https://static.standard.co.uk/s3fs-public/thumbnails/image/2016/02/22/16/fresh-meat.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Unsurprisingly, the number of young renters in London is falling. Hamptons research shows that renters aged under 25 make up just 12 per cent of tenants in London, down from a peak of one in five in 2011/12. In the past year alone the number of renters aged 16-24 fell by 11 per cent as more young people opt to stay living at home for longer. While there are clear financial incentives to do this, the arrangement has its downsides. “When you live at home, you pay with other things than money,” says 25-year-old Gargi, who moved from Copenhagen to London a year ago. “There’s a growth element in moving out.” Gargi, who works in consulting, took a pay cut to move to a more senior role in London. Whereas in Copenhagen she was paying 23 per cent of her income to rent a room in a shared home, now she pays closer to 37 per cent of her salary for the Hammersmith home she shares with three other similar-aged women. ![The cast of Crashing](https://static.standard.co.uk/s3fs-public/thumbnails/image/2016/01/07/16/crashing-channel-4.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) But she says the pull factors of the London lifestyle outweighed the financial negatives. “I really wanted to move to London for everything the city has to offer. I needed to expand my horizons. I’m connecting with new kinds of people and the work I do is on a wider, more global scale. “There’s always something to do, going out to eat, attending different events. I just went to The Weeknd concert and I had a friend who flew in from Copenhagen, whereas I just took the Metropolitan line, which is super cool because I used to fly in for those concerts before.” As Gargi acknowledges, though, the cost of renting combined with relatively low salaries does make it hard to enjoy everything the city has to offer. As Hamptons data found, in 2026 the average 22 to 29-year-old Londoner earns around £39,500 — although this can vary wildly depending on which sector they are employed in. This salary would allow them to spend approximately £1,086 per month on rent. On this basis, 38 per cent of newly let two-bedroom homes in London would be affordable to a couple, compared with 41 per cent in 2016, and down from a high of 49 per cent in 2018. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2023/01/18/13/Medium_71425_S3_Ep4_Stath%20Lets%20Flats%2C%20S3%2C%20Ep4-2.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Encouragingly, perhaps, the data did pinpoint 13 London boroughs where at least half of newly let two-bedroom homes would be affordable to two average young earners. If budget is key look to Sutton, Barking and Dagenham, Havering, Bromley, Croydon, Enfield, Redbridge, Waltham Forest, Lewisham, Hounslow, Barnet, Newham and Kingston upon Thames. Meanwhile, SpareRoom suggests renters who want to focus their search on the areas with the most homes to choose from should look east, to Docklands, Shoreditch and Bow, Stratford, West Ham and Bethnal Green. “Right now, east London offers both the highest supply and the cheapest rents in the capital, so it could be worth starting your search there,” says Hutchinson. “The faster you can move on viewings and paperwork, the better your chances of securing a great place to live.” The horror... the squalor... the joy! The Standard team remember their first flats in London Earlsfield Rent: £450 “We never used the downstairs loo again...” It was a drizzly November evening. The events of which are seared into my memory, but mostly my nostrils. I hadn’t long moved into a three-bedroom flat opposite the famous Henry Prince Estate with two friends when they suddenly acquired boyfriends. I was therefore largely abandoned and quite miserable. For £450 a month I resided in a dark, dank basement room next to the main bathroom. The loo being underground meant that it required a noisy pump to remove the waste and usher it to wherever yucky stuff like that is taken and converted into our drinking water. This particular night the pump failed — quite spectacularly. I also happened to be suffering from a stomach bug. Imagine my horror as I yanked the flush and the unpleasant deposit was violently churned up out of the bowl and onto the floor. Feeling poorly and sloshing around in sewage water, I had a little cry and then slid plastic bags onto my feet and spent the rest of the night cleaning it up. We never used the downstairs loo again. Suzannah Ramsdale Bethnal Green Rent: £349 “Once I pulled back the sofa to discover a pile of feathers — no bird body left, only feathers, which still disturbs me to this day.” I’ve lived in some horrible places in London. The Camden flat behind the Belgo kitchen with the “vat of fat” outside the front door. The Chalk Farm council house with a mouse problem only rivalled by its cockroach and ant issues; once I pulled back the sofa in this zoo from hell to discover a pile of feathers — no bird body left, only feathers, which still disturbs me to this day. But my very first house-share was on Paradise Row in Bethnal Green, and was quite marvellous. A five-storey townhouse with a bedroom on each floor, it was a lucky find providing a false idea of London living. Such things can’t last long, and hastened to an end after we decided to burn our Christmas tree on the gas fire. A midnight visit from big scary firemen slowly helped us comprehend that smoke was pouring into our neighbour’s house. A sobering moment: we weren’t ready for such a fine property. To the hovels! Martin Robinson Brixton Rent: £360 “It was like residing in Notting Hill but with a 365-day carnival in full force.” Stepping past the dodgy jerk chicken stall and through the unlit stock room of an old sports shop on Ferndale Road in Brixton to reach the door of the flat above should have been the red flag for us to look elsewhere. And as my friend Gary and I looked for new digs at the turn of the millennium, the letting agent’s embarrassed face became the second red flag. Having lived in Hackney in the 1990s, even that didn’t prepare me for the constant hive of activity in the heart of Brixton. It was like residing in Notting Hill but with a 365-day carnival in full force. The flat itself felt more like a rickety boat with its badly constructed wood-panelled walls, uneven floors and a toilet window (with no blinds) that faced on to the train track 15 feet away so we could wave at the passengers, while the smell of the jerk chicken and other local “herb” aromas filled our living space. But we loved it and it was cheap. Minutes from Brixton Academy and one of London’s best pubs (the Duke of Edinburgh, where I met my wife playing pool), with Jamaican patties on tap on most street corners (as well as retro dart boards in the store room) it soon became our haven. Ped Millichamp Clapham Rent: £530 “Googling ‘cheap rent for young woman in London’ remarkably led me to a normal house viewing instead of being murdered.” I didn’t find my absolute steal of a first London flat, my aunt did. In the summer of 2019, seeking to help me out ahead of my move, she punched “cheap rent for young woman in London” into Google, which remarkably led me to a normal house viewing instead of being murdered. Well, I say normal. The flat was located inside a disused military training building in between Clapham and Brixton, and it was the flatmates’ responsibility to live inside it to ward off potential squatters. Officially, we only had access to a 10th of the building, which comprised about seven bedrooms, two wonky bathrooms and a poky kitchen. Unofficially, we broke into the rest of the building regularly, hosting our house parties inside the haunted classrooms and full-scale basketball court (nary a ball was ever thrown, save for beer-pong). Occasionally I would return home after a night out with a friend or conquest and tour them around the spooky, cavernous halls, Second World War-style showers and sleeping quarters, complete with various abandoned bunk beds. It was a real aphrodisiac. Sadly it was bulldozed six months into me living there and is now a further education college. RIP. Maddy Mussen Crystal Palace Rent: £200 “My flatmate started asking that I keep my bedroom door open at night. Something to do with his cat, apparently. I moved out shortly after.” Even all those years ago, £200 a month was cheap. Remarkably so. What did I have to do for the landlord in return? Look after his beloved cat, mostly, while he went to Finland or Pakistan for work, which he did quite a lot. He seemed like an OK bloke, if a little timid and quiet. Enjoyed computer games. Often went to Tooting for curry. I was working in Shoreditch at the time, mostly for Business Insider and Vice, so wasn’t at the flat much. I’d leave fairly early — quite a long walk to Crystal Palace overground — and then go to the pub or one of the then en vogue Shoreditch cocktail bars after work. I probably wouldn’t have been able to go out much at all had my rent been a normal rate. Balance; pay-offs. I quite liked living that far south, on the Croydon side — it was near much of my family and felt homely and comfortable. Sunday lunch at nonna’s didn’t require a schlep. And I was close to Selhurst Park, home to the mighty Crystal Palace, and Tasty Jerk, which serves one hell of a Jamaican barbecue. But then my flatmate started asking that I keep my bedroom door open at night. Something to do with his cat, apparently. I moved out shortly after. Josh Barrie Warwick Avenue Rent: £0 “No rug, duvet or blanket was safe from the dog. Then there was the freezer, which was inexplicably full of monkey poo…” I thought I’d struck gold when a friend offered me her parents’ beautiful Maida Vale townhouse, instead of an expensive flatshare I couldn’t afford, while doing work experience. Her parents were former hippies who had squatted there in the 1960s and later bought the house for next to nothing under squatters’ rights. By the time I stayed there, it was worth millions, and they liked to share their good fortune. In many ways, it was ideal. I only paid the bills, it was central, and the house was incredible. The catch was the dog: a sweet but completely untrained creature who was blind, deaf, and apparently beyond the reach of discipline. At least once a day — usually when I was bleary-eyed and heading for the shower — I’d step in a fresh pile of poo. No rug, duvet or blanket was safe. The family’s generosity extended well beyond me. The house seemed to operate as an unofficial care-in-the-community scheme. Window cleaners would appear unannounced, splash some dirty water around, and ask for money. Cleaners would sit at the kitchen table smoking for an hour. A gardener once drank several of my beers before asking for money. Then there was the freezer, which was inexplicably full of monkey poo. My friend’s mother spent much of her time away studying monkeys and, improbably, writing lesbian erotica. I remain grateful for the place. Still, I was surprisingly pleased when it was time to leave and move into a lodging with no kitchen, no sitting room and a grieving widow. But that’s another story. Harriet Addison Barons Court Rent: £400 “There wasn’t any central heating and no shower. I lasted six weeks.” I moved into my bargain Barons Court flat sometime in the mid 2010s full of postgraduate hope. A friend of a friend had discovered an all-girls’ flatshare inside a handsome Victorian red brick, and a room had just come up. The labyrinthine top-floor flat was owned by a woman we only ever knew as “Granny”. She no longer lived in London but was keen to rent out the rooms in her eccentric flat to give young girls moving to London a chance. It was only £400 a month, cash, and all we had to deal with were several rooms full of dusty portraits and antique curiosities. That, and the fact that there wasn’t any central heating and no shower — just one bath shared between four. I went to view the flat one evening just before Christmas, and my festive beer jacket and youthful naivety assured me that these were minor issues. The hardy Barons Court girls didn’t need fancy mod cons. We would hide in The Curtains Up pub for warmth, flirt with boys from nearby Queen’s Club Gardens, or use some of the rent money we’d be saving on weekly blow-dries in lieu of showers. And we could be on the Piccadilly line to our unpaid internships in minutes. Granny’s was a rare gem; it would be like a charming modern dorm for upstart west London millennials trying to make it in the big city. Reader: I lasted six weeks. But I did have great hair for the duration. Jessica Burrell Stockwell Rent: £550 each “Shambling to the shop for Alka-Seltzer felt especially shameful when you passed impeccably dressed churchgoers” What’s worse than hangover guilt? Hangover guilt soundtracked by the fervent, soaring voices of a gospel congregation, harmonising 10 feet below your pounding head. The first London flat I rented with my now-husband was in the part of Stockwell estate agents like to call the “Clapham North Triangle”, opposite the Landor (excellent beer), down the road from a Cuban bar (excellent mojitos) and above a gospel church (excellent singing). The problem with this combination was that the hymns happened on a Sunday morning, just as we emerged from a mojito- or beer-induced fug. Shambling to the shop for Alka-Seltzer/Berocca/salt and vinegar crisps felt especially shameful when you passed impeccably dressed churchgoers after the service; nothing like encountering a lady in a powder blue hat, skirt suit and matching handbag while you wipe last night’s eyeliner off your face to make you ponder your life choices. The flat’s other unique selling point was the way you reached it — along a badly lit alleyway and up a rickety metal staircase that finally cracked on the day we moved out. Still, we were lucky: our landlord was a friend who charged us £1,100 a month and was sympathetic to our litany of domestic disasters, which culminated in the shower screen falling off the wall one day when my school friend, over from Paris, was mid hair-wash. The safety glass smashed into a thousand pieces, one of which ended up embedded in her calf. Better a leg than an eye; maybe all that singing had granted us some grace. Fiona Roberts-Moore
summary: Young graduates moving to London face an increasingly difficult rental market characterized by rising costs, low starter salaries, and shrinking housing supply. With the average inner London room costing £979 per month, many young adults spend over half of their income on rent or choose to live at home longer. Despite these financial and competitive hurdles, many young renters still value the vibrant lifestyle and career opportunities the capital offers.
key_points: The average monthly cost for a room in inner London is £979.
Rental supply in London has dropped due to increased landlord taxes and the Renters’ Rights Act.
The proportion of renters aged under 25 in London has declined to 12 percent, down from a peak of 20 percent in 2011/12.
East London currently offers some of the highest rental supply and cheapest rents in the capital.

title: ‘I graduated from a top London university, 100 applications later I’m still jobless’
author: Holly Evans
content:
On paper, it should have straight forward for Emily Shulman to secure a job upon graduating from her journalism master’s degree at Goldsmiths University in London.
The 22-year-old had already achieved an undergraduate degree in criminology and sociology from the University of Nottingham, and has a host of work experiences and internships under her belt.
However, more than 100 applications later and she remains unemployed and is among the one million young people struggling to settle into a career.
“At first it was instant rejections but as I did more work experience, I got more interviews but ultimately everything was leading to nothing,” she told The Independent.
“I’ve tried different approaches such as reaching out to people on LinkedIn, applying online, emailing - but so often I’ve been ghosted.”
Recent official figures showed the number of vacancies in the UK jobs market fell to a five-year low in the three months to July.
![Around one in eight people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Alamy/PA)](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/05/27/22/27192738-e994dd98-e7a5-4997-b6ff-f3a826cf3fca.jpg)
The latest Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey found that small firms may not be recruiting because of increased labour costs and other business expenses, while the war in the Middle East has caused economic uncertainty and rising living costs.
This has particularly impacted young people, with the latest data, published earlier this year, showing the number of people aged between 16 and 24 and not in employment, education or training – so-called Neets – was at nearly one million.
“I think a lot of people are in the same position as me,” Ms Shulman said. “My sister is one year older and she did a law conversion and couldn’t get a training contract. She’s ended up moving to Manchester and doing something law-related but not what she really wanted to do.
“A lot of my friends from my master’s are still unemployed. It’s so hard anyways going from living independently in university to living with your parents. The cost of London makes socialising so hard, going on a night out together is especially hard when you have no income.”
She has since carried out a number of unpaid internships in order to gain as much work experience as possible, but says the job market is “oversaturated” and that many advertisements require several years of experience for junior roles.
Another issue named by those applying is the presence of “ghost jobs”. This refers to the practice of employers or recruiters advertising roles which may already have been filled or may not have existed in the first place.
The purpose of this is often to build a pool of candidates for future hiring, or to keep a list of names incase the recent hire doesn’t work out.
![Ms Shulman has done a number of internships and has both a Masters and an undergraduate degree](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/10/10/09/unnamed.jpg)
A report published by City Hall in April found that artificial intelligence was threatening at least a million jobs in London alone, mainly administrative roles and jobs in areas such as IT and data analysis.
Women, who are overrepresented in administrative and clerical roles, young people and those with higher educational levels are among the most exposed, the report states.
“I try to stay optimistic but it is really disheartening, especially when you can’t celebrate your achievements,” Ms Shulman said. “I was coming to the end of my Masters but that looming deadline of September and having nothing to show for it clouded everything.
“You feel you can’t be excited until you know what you’re doing,” she said.
The ONS said its early estimates show there were around 6,000 fewer vacancies between May and July, compared with February to April.
This brings the level of vacancies down to 707,000, the lowest in more than five years or, outside of the Covid pandemic years, since 2014.
Vacancies slumped earlier in the year in a sign that firms were pulling back hiring in the face of economic uncertainty and higher wage costs.
![Spencer Stern has applied to over 200 jobs since he left his data analyst role in July 2025](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/10/10/35/2206d140-a850-49af-9f91-f96e95abd345.jpg)
It isn’t just graduates who are struggling to find secure employment. Spencer Stern, 44, spent nine years as a senior data analyst before leaving his role last summer, but has now applied to over 200 jobs in his ongoing search.
“Sometimes I just get frustrated and fire off applications and not care,” he said. “You’ve got these AI ‘easy apply’ type jobs which I’ve found quite rubbish. It’s just shooting applications into a black hole. They are essentially flooding the recruiters with CVs which makes it even harder for those who are not using auto-apply apps.”
He added: “In terms of difficulties in the job market, it’s gone from a handful of stages to a ridiculous amount of stages. You now have to apply with a cover letter and a questionnaire, then a one-way video interview, a test, a call with a recruiter, a hiring manager, a take home task and a presentation before in-person interviews.”
As a result, Mr Stern is channelling his energy into building his own venture ChatbotCV, which he hopes will help employers filter through CVs for the relevant information.
“One of the most devastating things about being out of work is the unstructured time,” he said. “It’s devastating on the mind so over time I’ve had to structure my thoughts and figure out something that’s keeping me busy, in a way that I can hopefully monetise.”
A DWP spokesperson said: “Every young person deserves the chance to build a future they can be proud of, and we are reforming Jobcentres so they are better able to support those including graduates trying to find work.
“Thanks to our £2.5 billion investment, there are more opportunities opening up for those looking to take the next step in their career, supporting almost one million young people and unlocking up to 500,000 jobs and training opportunities.
“Businesses also receive significant tax breaks through the national insurance exemption for under-21s and apprentices under 25, alongside hiring incentives worth up to £8,000 when they take on an eligible young person.”
summary: Emily Shulman, a 22-year-old graduate with two degrees and multiple internships, remains unemployed after submitting more than 100 job applications amidst a tough UK job market. Official figures show that UK job vacancies have fallen to a five-year low, disproportionately affecting young people and nearly one million so-called 'Neets.' Job seekers face additional hurdles including oversaturated markets, lengthy interview processes, 'ghost jobs,' and the rising influence of artificial intelligence.
key_points: UK job vacancies fell to a five-year low in the three months to July, contributing to economic difficulties for job seekers.
Nearly one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are currently not in education, employment, or training.
Job applicants face widespread challenges such as being ghosted, navigating 'ghost jobs,' and dealing with increasingly lengthy recruitment processes.
A City Hall report indicated that artificial intelligence threatens at least one million jobs in London, particularly impacting young people and highly educated individuals.

title: Seven teens and man arrested for attempted murder over 'machete fight' at KFC
author: Matt Watts
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Helicopter seen hovering above Bromley after four stabbed on high street]() ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) The brawl on Bromley High Street, in southeast London, unfolded shortly after 2pm on Thursday and left a 21-year-old man in a critical condition. He was rushed to hospital along with three boys, aged between 14 and 17, who were also stabbed. After medical assessment, his injuries have since been deemed non-life-threatening. He has since been arrested along with the boys who were stabbed. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/19/01M2640K8E4QACRYYEAD6CW2KM.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Witnesses described loud bangs and screams of horror as the altercation — feared to be between two rival local gangs — took place. A cafe worker reported seeing “boys running with long knives” at the scene of the crime on Thursday. Speaking to the Metro, the unnamed worked said: “People were scattering everywhere....Everyone was terrified.” ![

Police Community Support Officers at the scene in Bromley

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/11/01M2640HF4XCD3AKJ7A79MY6M4.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Forensic officers and a crime scene photographer were later seen working inside and outside the KFC restaurant on the High Street and there were evidence markers on the floor. The fast food chain confirmed a “serious incident” took place inside their restaurant. Officers rushed to the London high street to reports of an “altercation” at around 2.15pm on Thursday and the four males stabbed were taken to hospital. ![

The scene after four people were stabbed on Bromley High Street

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/17/13/Screenshot-2026-09-10-180638.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Local MP Peter Fortune said police had informed him there is "no further risk to the public". ![

Forensic investigators at the scene

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/09/01M264AXMWV2P2S6M55WYW0R6K.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Chief Inspector David Cooper, who leads policing in the local area, said:“We recognise the impact this incident will have on the local community, and officers are working quickly to establish the full circumstances. “There will be an increased police presence in the area, and we encourage anyone with information or concerns to speak to officers.” Officers are appealing to anyone who may have footage or information relating to the incident to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 4008/10SEP, or Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.
summary: Seven teenagers and a man have been arrested for attempted murder following a violent machete fight near a KFC on Bromley High Street in southeast London. The altercation on Thursday afternoon resulted in four males being stabbed, including a 21-year-old man initially in critical condition and three boys aged 14 to 17. Police confirmed all four injured individuals have been arrested, while local authorities assured the public that there is no further risk.
key_points: A brawl on Bromley High Street at around 2pm on Thursday involved individuals with long knives.
Four males were stabbed, including a 21-year-old man and three boys aged between 14 and 17.
Seven teenagers and a man were arrested for attempted murder, which includes the injured parties.
Police and forensic officers investigated the scene inside and outside a KFC restaurant.
Local MP Peter Fortune stated that police informed him there is no further risk to the public.

title: Portsmouth Sam Smith support act talks of 'gorgeous' experience
author: Galya Dimitrova
content:
![Bradley Jago and Sam Smith smiling as they meet. They have their hands on each other's arms.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/835/cpsprodpb/a826/live/a5681940-ad39-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg)
Jago describes Sam Smith as "the most genuine, warm, kind person"
- Published
"I've been so much more nervous for much smaller gigs."
Portsmouth musician Bradley Jago was one of the 10 acts chosen to support Sam Smith in London and Manchester, as part of the singer's UK-wide talent search with BBC Introducing.
Jago made it through more than 1,500 submissions and said meeting Sam Smith had been "gorgeous and they were just exactly who I thought they would be".
He said stepping on the stage at the London Coliseum, he had felt "calm" and it "just felt right".
![A black-and-white image of Bradley Jago singing on stage.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/942d/live/f5fd70f0-ad37-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg)
Bradley Jago said writing music was "my therapy, it's what I need to do"
Sam Smith's residencies follow the release of their latest album, Hazel Eyes, in August.
The multi award-winning musician will play at the London Coliseum for eight nights, from 8 until 19 September.
"I was strangely calm and I really wasn't expecting it," said Jago, who performed on the opening night.
"I was all week, I've been crazy, I've been all over the place.
"But then ... the time had come and everything aligned and I just honestly enjoyed it so so much, and took it all in."
He said he had got to meet Smith and described them as "the most genuine, warm, kind person".
"They say don't meet your idols, but it lived up to it."
The Portsmouth artist, who is part of the LGBT community, said he always described his music as "queer soul for queer souls, but truly it is for everyone".
"I think queerness is a very all-encompassing label," he said.
"I actually write music for me, it's my therapy, it's what I need to do."
He said people connected to the way he expressed himself.
"Which is gorgeous and there've been songs that I think are a really niche kind of queer experience and then I've had hundreds of comments on TikTok saying I've been through exactly this.
"This is why it's so important to talk about because other people have been through this."
Smith said the discovery process for artists and audiences "is so important and being able to play a part in that is fantastic".
summary: Portsmouth musician Bradley Jago was chosen from over 1,500 submissions to support Sam Smith at the London Coliseum as part of a BBC Introducing talent search. Jago described the experience of meeting Smith and performing on stage as gorgeous and surprisingly calm. Jago characterizes his music as "queer soul" and views songwriting as a form of personal therapy.
key_points: Portsmouth musician Bradley Jago was one of 10 acts chosen to support Sam Smith in London and Manchester.
Jago was selected after beating more than 1,500 submissions in a BBC Introducing talent search.
He described meeting Sam Smith as living up to expectations, calling them genuine, warm, and kind.
Jago described his music as queer soul and considers writing music to be his therapy.

title: Sadiq Khan ‘plans to ban wood-burning stoves in parts of London’ in clean air push
author: Nicole Wootton-Cane
content:
Sadiq Khan is pushing to ban wood-burning stoves in parts of London as he ramps up clean air efforts in the capital, according to reports.
The Mayor of London wants to create specific zero-emissions zones where log-burning stoves, bonfires, and the burning of “solid fuels” would be restricted in private homes and gardens.
The Telegraph reports Lord Khan has urged the government to give him and other local authority leaders more power to crack down on solid fuel burning by allowing them to ban the stoves.
![Lord Khan has brought in a raft of clean air measures since becoming Mayor of London](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/04/12/01M1P2XAZAEHJDDTMBA12DVDK5.jpg)
In a formal submission to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), Lord Khan requested to be able to enforce tougher rules in London.
Current restrictions mean he can create smoke control areas on council property, such as parks and allotments, but stop short of banning people from burning dry logs in wood burners that meet the current efficiency rules.
It comes after researchers warned burning wood indoors could cause damage akin to cigarette smoke as a new study linked the growing popularity of domestic wood burning to lung damage. Experts from University College London (UCL) said domestic wood burning is a major source of PM2.5 air pollution – tiny particles that penetrate deep into the lungs.
The Mayor has made London’s air quality a priority during his time in office, most notably by introducing the Ultra Low Emissions Zone (Ulez) in 2019. A recent study estimated a 40 per cent reduction in deaths linked to toxic air across the capital over the five years between the beginning of the scheme and 2024.
He has since argued for the further expansion of the Ulez scheme, saying there is “more to do”.
“The evidence is now overwhelming and unarguable: the bold action we have taken in London has reduced pollution, improved public health and saved lives,” he said following the results of the study earlier this year.
![Researchers warned burning wood indoors could cause damage akin to cigarette smoke](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/01/23/9/07/wood-burning-stove-stock.jpeg)
“From childhood asthma to dementia, we know what a wide range of illnesses are linked to air pollution. This latest data shows why expanding Ulez London-wide was even more important than we previously thought and is transforming lives right across our capital.
