![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Much of the rest of England and Wales has also seen temperatures in the mid-20s, while parts of central and southern Europe have been baked in intense heat, with some spots exceeding 45C.
On Thursday, Huelva in Spain reached a staggering 45.7C, as the country experienced its hottest day of 2026.
The warmth in the capital, however, will be short-lived according to upcoming forecasts.
Temperatures for the forthcoming week suggest highs in the low 20s, with the possibility of showers.
Tuesday seems set to be breezy with sunny spells, followed by a windy Wednesday and a dry Thursday, with light winds and hazy sunshine.
Longer term, the national forecaster suggests that London should expect some longer dry spells as we head toward mid-September.
Temperatures will probably be close to average overall, though still with some relatively cool nights at times.
summary: London and much of England and Wales have experienced a warm autumn spell with temperatures nearing 28C, contrasting with intense heat exceeding 45C in parts of southern and central Europe. However, this warm weather in the capital will be short-lived, with upcoming forecasts predicting highs in the low 20s and potential showers next week. Longer-term forecasts indicate London can expect longer dry spells toward mid-September with temperatures close to average.
key_points: London and parts of England and Wales saw warm temperatures nearing 28C and the mid-20s.
Huelva in Spain reached a staggering 45.7C on Thursday, marking the country's hottest day of 2026.
Forecasts for the upcoming week in London predict lower highs in the low 20s and possible showers.
The national forecaster expects longer dry spells for London heading toward mid-September with near-average temperatures.

title: For the first time in 350 years, this historic London landmark could be getting a visitor centre
author: Katie Forge
content:
![A side by side image of the monument in the city of London](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/04104518/Copy-of-FACEBOOK-SPLIT-IMAGE-59-1024x576.png) 
Whilst London certainly isn’t thin on the ground when it comes to its legendary landmarks, only one of the city’s many monuments is the Monument. Built to honour one of the most significant events in British history, this tall stone column was created as a commemoration of the Great Fire of London – and has been proudly overlooking the Square Mile for 350 years now.
Perched just 62 metres away from Pudding Lane (the very spot in which the Great Fire broke out in 1666), the Monument was designed by iconic architect, Christopher Wren, alongside scientist, Dr Robert Hooke. Built from Portland stone across a six-year period, the Monument officially opened to the public in 1677 as a celebration of the city’s resurgence – and now stands as a much-loved legacy of Old London.
Approximately 200,000 people ascend the structure’s spiral staircase each year to feast their eyes on one of the very best views in London. But that number could soon reach new heights, because – for the first time in 350 years – the Monument could be getting an actual visitor centre.
![The monument commemorating the Great Fire of London](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/04110113/The_Monument_-_geograph.org_.uk_-_3087765-1024x714.jpg)
The Monument currently only boasts a small entrance and ticket desk, but the demolition of the structure’s next door neighbour could pave the way for a ground-floor visitor centre. The building in question is Faryners House, a Brutalist-style structure that was named after the baker who may (or may not) have started the Great Fire of London. The demolition of this building would make room for a new office – but the redevelopment plans could also feature a dedicate visitor space.
The proposed plans come courtesy of the architectural aficionados over at Fletcher Priest Architects. Inside the prospective visitor centre, there would be be an exhibition about the Great Fire of London and a cafe. Plans are still very much in the early stages, but if they are approved, construction could start next year. And the Monument could be welcoming its shiny new visitor centre shortly after.
summary: The historic Monument in London, which commemorates the Great Fire of London, may receive its first-ever visitor centre after 350 years. Proposed by Fletcher Priest Architects, the new space would feature a cafe and an exhibition about the Great Fire. The project is made possible by the planned demolition of the neighbouring Faryners House.
key_points: The Monument was designed by Christopher Wren and Dr Robert Hooke to commemorate the Great Fire of London.
Approximately 200,000 people visit the structure annually.
The proposed visitor centre depends on the demolition of the neighbouring Faryners House.
Plans for the centre include an exhibition about the Great Fire and a cafe.
Construction could begin next year if the early-stage plans are approved.

title: Beyond the tourist traps: How top chefs are revamping London's Southbank
author: Josh Barrie
content:
The Southbank renaissance: This time it's for locals
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![The London Question: Should London have a tourist tax?](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/15/Sea-Containers-restaurant.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![The London List](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_going_out_embed_desktop.png)
It’s Saturday on the South Bank and crowds are heaving. The London Eye, almost as old as the first Giraffe World Kitchen restaurant (1998, Hampstead), feels almost old amid all the selfies and Lime bikes. Tourists weave between hot-dog vendors and doughnut stands. Some find respite in the entrance to Sea Life, a once grand aquarium now easily missed along the thoroughfare, and others queue for the London Dungeon, which moved from its more fittingly sinister location in the belly of London Bridge to County Hall in 2013.
The South Bank hasn’t been considered a cool part of town for decades. No district of London with an attraction called Shrek’s Adventure! can possibly inspire reverence or inspire prolonged visits from actual Londoners.
That’s not to say there aren’t cultural touchstones here: the Southbank Centre, the National Theatre, Shakespeare’s Globe, the BFI and Tate Modern are some of London’s best ports of call. They’re world famous, in fact. But it isn’t them, it’s the overall feel of the place — the “vibe” in modern terms — and much of that can be pinned to food and drink. You can enjoy Hockney or Hamlet but you’ll be back over the river to Soho for a drink afterwards, or east to Borough Market for dinner (merhaba, Kismet; bonjour Camille).
Or you would have until recently. These days, increasingly, the South Bank has options. It’s changing, evolving; people are starting to realise that all this brutalism, contemporary art and theatrical stardom is deserving of more than Wagamama, Strada and La Gamba.
These might be fine, to a point — let’s not be snobbish. After all, accessible chains are generally willing and able to cough up for the soaring rents and why wouldn’t they invest in a site with riverside views? But they’re not exciting; they hardly match up to Shakespeare.
Enter Gordon Ramsay. He’s gambling on a venture at Sea Containers, a hotel and restaurant en vogue 10 years ago but much less talked about on the London scene today.
![Sea Containers restaurant](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/15/Sea-Containers-restaurant.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
And he’s not opened one of his affordable burger bars or pizza joints. It’s a fully fledged restaurant, serving tagliolini with crab from Brixham, Devon, and his famous beef Wellington. And sure, there are crowd-pleasers.
This isn’t food for Michelin inspectors. His Idiot Sandwich Flight, at £26, attests to that. But it’s a big opening, and it’s a marker in the South Bank sand.
Growing football at the Southbank
“Opening a restaurant on London’s South Bank this month feels like the perfect time,” Ramsay tells me while on a flight from the US. “It’s one of the most multicultural and vibrant stretches of the capital — a place where the river brings people together, where street food, cafés and restaurants sit alongside music, theatre and art.”
Ramsay is classically upbeat. Why wouldn’t he be? This is a part of London with a monster footfall; one which, even if Londoners don’t buy into it, will entice an endless deluge of tourists regardless. Last year, South Bank BID, which lobbies for business interests in the area, reported 38 million visitors, representing a 20 per cent growth over two years. But there also seems to be a sense that Londoners are, at least in part, reclaiming this stretch of riverside too. It should be for everyone.
“It’s one of the most multicultural and vibrant stretches of the capital”
Gordon Ramsay
Ramsay adds: “Food here isn’t simply something you eat — it’s part of the culture, the conversation and the energy of the riverside. It’s exciting and that is exactly why we wanted to be here.”
Read More
Ramsay isn’t the only high-profile hospitality man banking on the place. Soon, Jack Croft and Will Murray, of Fallow, one of London’s most lauded restaurants (500,000 Instagram followers and counting), will put their own stamp on the South Bank, albeit in a different guise to Fallow.
Together with business partner James Robson, who’s also led the group to open Roe, in Canary Wharf, and Fowl in Mayfair, they’ve taken on the restaurant space at the Oxo Tower, a landmark that first launched as a hospitality space in 1996. Robson says there’s a “new energy” to the South Bank and taking on the Oxo Tower was ultimately a “no-brainer in 2026”.
![Fallow, soon to be at Oxo Tower](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/48/Fallow-Southbank.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“There’s definitely something happening in the area,” he tells the Standard. “I got the call that the venue was for sale while on holiday, a quick approach, and we owned it 18 days later.
“We moved ultra-fast because it’s an amazing site in an area with enormous potential. The views are incredible.”
Robson says the team won’t be installing a branch of Fallow at the location. Instead, they’ll play to the strengths of the place, separating the 12,500 sq ft site into a chic brasserie on one side and, possibly, a more casual offering on the other. Much is still to be decided, he says. Either way, the current restaurant and bar is to be revamped and updated.
“We’ll be polishing up the offering, giving it more value and a lot more love,” he says. “We’ll lean into the brand too and create something by our chefs. I think there’ll be an elevated concept on one side, and then we’ll draw on the history on the other. We’ve gone in fast, but we always think very carefully.”
Is there money to be made here, beyond the churn of chains and the stream of modest street food vans? “The restaurant is turning over about £10 million a year at the moment.
“Hopefully we’ll double that to get into profit. They’re losing money at the moment. We can turn it around, invest and sharpen the place up; get some economies of scale going. I really think the South Bank is on fire.”
Restaurants are flocking to the area
Robson mentions other restaurant brands soon to arrive. Caravan, a growing group of brunch-style restaurants founded by the Kiwi trio Miles Kirby, Laura Harper-Hinton and Chris Ammermann, is opening at the Southbank Centre, on the terrace, in the old Ping Pong location, in November.
“Borough Market isn’t far away either,” Robson adds. “And there are street food vans everywhere, which is great for passing trade.”
With food and drink comes commerce. It’s little wonder other industries are identifying a blossoming landscape, one that will feed London’s office workers well, as well as affordably and conveniently. Next year, the Lego Group will move its London hub from Farringdon to the South Bank, taking on a 192,000 sq ft space over three and half floors. It shows intent.
Loren I Shuster, chief people officer for Lego, said of the move last May: “We’re excited about moving to the South Bank.
“It’s the cultural heart of London, which makes it the perfect location for a company dedicated to inspiring creativity. 76 Southbank is an iconic building.” Kudos, then, to those with the foresight to have come in early.
“It’s the cultural heart of London”
Loren I Shuster
One is Lasdun, which opened in the National Theatre way back in 2023. If anything, fanfare around the venture wasn’t frenzied enough at the time — judging by today’s standards, anyway, where restaurants are exalted as if Mayan gods — though it did get a four-star review from then Standard critic Jimi Famurewa, and a similarly joyful write-up from Grace Dent. Anyway, Lasdun is the work of Jon Rotheram, Tom Harris and John Ogier, the trio behind the critically acclaimed Hackney pub The Marksman. Today the £32 pre-theatre menu features dishes such as Cornish fish soup, smoked haddock fishcakes and slow-roast Hereford beef with bobby beans and mustard.
Forza had been a part of Peckham’s dining fabric for years, but there came a time to grow. The South Bank was where co-founders and childhood friends Bash Redford and Michael Lavery pitched up (they’ve since opened another restaurant in Soho).
![Forza Wine at the National Theatre](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/39/Forza-Wine-at-the-National-Theatre-PR-shot-CREDIT-Caitlin-Isola.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Redford says: “I don’t want this to sound like a PR soundbite, but I think the South Bank is turning into a place that Londoners want to go. It’s still a place for visitors and tourists, obviously, but ours is a restaurant for locals too. It’s a balancing act. We have to think about everyone.
“For a long time, our nearest competitor was Giraffe. Before we came here, I could count the number of times I’d visited the South Bank on one hand. I suppose it was a prospect, but a gamble too. But we thought, maybe we can make this work.”
Forza Wine can be found on the first floor of the National Theatre. It boasts an enviable terrace overlooking Waterloo Bridge, Embankment and, newly, Nick Jones’ St Clement hotel. Things are happening on both sides of the river.
“We planned it out and we were excited about the footfall,” Redford says. “I do think there’s long been an element of customers playing it safe. Maybe the younger crowd go to known brands and older ones stick to Pizza Express or Brasserie Blanc (Raymond Blanc’s casual chain).
“But we were excited at the time, about the footfall and what we could achieve. I think there’s change happening here and it’s very much a case of ‘the more the merrier’.
“Maybe this part of London was forgotten by the people who live here. There was snobbery around it. Not so much now.”
summary: London's South Bank is experiencing a culinary renaissance, moving away from generic chains and tourist traps to attract top-tier chefs and local diners. High-profile hospitality ventures led by Gordon Ramsay, the team behind Fallow, Caravan, and Forza Wine are revamping spaces across the district. Alongside these new dining options, the area is drawing major commercial interest, including a future move by the Lego Group.
key_points: Gordon Ramsay has opened a full-scale restaurant at Sea Containers on the South Bank, featuring dishes like Brixham crab tagliolini and beef Wellington.
The team behind Fallow has taken over the restaurant space at the Oxo Tower to create a new concept featuring a chic brasserie and a casual offering.
Other notable brands like Caravan and Forza Wine are establishing a presence in the area to appeal to both tourists and locals.
The South Bank BID reported 38 million visitors last year, representing a 20 percent growth over two years.
The Lego Group is scheduled to move its London hub to a large space on the South Bank next year.

title: West London council left disabled man without necessary therapies for 14 months
author: Philip James Lynch; Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/05/11/33/IMG_2016-(1).JPG?trim=252,0,252,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000>)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
The council failed to review the man’s (referred to as Mr B in the report) ECHP after he had moved to the area during his transition into adulthood.
In spring 2025, Mr B’s family moved to the borough with an ECHP – a plan which stated that Mr B should attend an independent special school and receive direct in-class support from a speech and language therapist.
The Local Government Ombudsman found this to be a fault on the part of Ealing Council, arguing that “the council should have reviewed Mr B’s EHC Plan by July 2025”.
The council responded to the complaint, outlining that Mr B would receive tuition in the meantime while the council finds him an independent school. All councils have a duty to make sure a young person with an EHCP receives the special educational provision set out in their plan.
Ealing Council should have made provision available in April, yet failed to until October 2025 – deemed as fault number two. By July 2026, Ealing Council still had yet to issue its finalised EHCP.
In January 2026, the local authority assessed that Mr B needed the support of a personal assistant to access his tuition. The information it referred to in its decision-making was available in April 2025, leading the watchdog to conclude that ”the council could have completed this assessment earlier”.
Mr X also complained about poor communication from Ealing Council. The authority put this down to a “staffing issue” and has apologised for this.
Read More
The Ombudsman issued a number of actions the council must take to remedy the situation. It ordered that within eight weeks of the final decision, published in July 2026, Mr B’s ECHP must be issued.
It has told the council to arrange speech and language therapy and take action to address the shortfall in the provision caused by the 14-month delay. The authority must also arrange and address occupational therapy after the 14 months without.
Ealing Council has agreed to apologise to Mr X and Mr B, and will make a payment of £500 compensation. An Ealing Council spokesperson said: “We accept the Ombudsman’s findings and apologise for the delays experienced by this young person and their family.
“We have agreed to the recommendations, including issuing the final Education Health and Care (EHC) Plan, ensuring the required support is in place, provided a formal apology and made the recommended payment. We are also working to improve how we plan and manage transitions from children’s to adult services for young people with EHC Plans.”
summary: Ealing Council was found at fault by the Local Government Ombudsman for leaving a disabled man without necessary therapies and an updated Education, Health and Care Plan for 14 months during his transition into adulthood. The watchdog concluded the council failed to review his plan, delayed educational provisions, and dragged out assessments despite having the relevant information available. The council has accepted the findings, apologized to the family, agreed to pay £500 in compensation, and committed to issuing the final plan and arranging the required therapy shortfalls.
key_points: Ealing Council failed to review Mr B's EHCP after his family moved to the borough in spring 2025.
The local authority left the disabled man without necessary therapies and provisions for a period of 14 months.
The council delayed assessing the need for a personal assistant for tuition, despite relevant information being available since April 2025.
The Local Government Ombudsman ordered the council to issue the final EHCP, arrange speech and language and occupational therapies, and address the provision shortfalls.
Ealing Council accepted the Ombudsman's findings, apologized, agreed to pay £500 compensation, and pledged to improve adult transition services.

title: A renovation of two halves: how a perfect family home took time
author: Prudence Ivey
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Tom Boland in his north-west London home](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/12/Tom-Boland-in-his-north-west-London-home.jpeg?trim=105,0,105,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![Homes & Property](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_hnp_embed_desktop.png)
Trying to find Aperture House on a residential street in north-west London, I walk past the address several times. The door number matches the one I have been given, but the kerb appeal is… not what I am expecting from the big-budget, architect-led renovation I have been sent images of. Nonetheless, not discovering a parallel house with the same door number, I try my luck and ring the bell.
“When people come over for the first time they often ask if we’re planning to leave the front like this to deter burglars,” laughs Tom Boland, as he opens the undeniably decrepit front door onto a scene far more in line with what I was expecting. “It’s more that we’re lazy, and also we want to take the whole thing back to brick and so, again, you’ve got to find £20,000 and it is just not top of our mission.”
This trade-off is emblematic of Tom, a journalist and his psychiatrist husband Billy’s entire approach to renovating the house they now share with their 18-month-old daughter. A reluctance to compromise on finishes and specification meant they had to approach the work in two phases (with more to come) in order to manage their budget, something Studio McW, the architecture practice they enlisted to help them, says has become more common with rising construction costs.
The couple bought the Edwardian end-of-terrace house in 2019 and lived in it in a state of some disrepair through the first Covid lockdown, planning all the ways they wanted to change it. When builders upped tools again, the couple jumped in at the deep end, opting to tackle the most overwhelming part of their home makeover first. “The kitchen was in the worst shape and was the least liveable part of the house,” explains Tom. The pair wanted to extend, rather than just refurbish the existing decrepit 1970s layout, so they felt free to make bolder architectural choices than in the rest of the house, where they were planning to respect the period bones. The north-facing room was very dark so introducing as much light as possible was a priority. They built out at the back with fairly standard floor-to-ceiling glazing. Studio McW also designed them a less conventional, chapel-like, pyramidal-roofed side extension with an oculus allowing light to enter from above.
![Tom Boland with his architect Greg Walton](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/28/Tom-Boland-with-his-architect-Greg-Walton.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
A small internal courtyard, bordered on three sides by the extension, the living room and a small shower room, draws light into all three spaces and offers a green outlook. Tom says adding the courtyard was a “challenging decision. It’s not really used, we don’t go out and sit there and mentally we had to give up square footage but actually I find it really pleasing. It is a focal point and that tends to be a more quiet, reflective part of the house now. We’re lucky that the proportions and size of the house allow us to have moments like this.”
A large oak storage wall partitions the kitchen and the living dining area. A large opening is carved through the centre of the structure providing a very child-friendly climbing nook, soon to have cushions added for more seating overlooking the courtyard. It also provides another through sight line to the house. “The entire design principle for Studio McW was that you could stand in the front of the house and just about see through to the garden. That was always the kind of driving principle of the design,” says Tom.
The couple thought the kitchen was going to be the most expensive part of the refurb and so hoped to get their significant spending out of the way. “I wildly underestimated what this was going to cost, partly because I realised throughout the process that I wasn’t really willing to compromise on what I wanted to do. You’re meant to add 20 per cent contingency but I think we were well over that,” says Tom. Suggestions that a door could hinge rather than pivot, or that adding a shadow gap between the tiled skirting and the wall might be too complex only crystallised for Tom just how much he cared about the finish and materiality.
![Tom Boland property](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/43/Tom-Boland-property.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
There was a planning objection to the height of the extension, so they dug down a metre into the ground rather than compromise on ceiling height. “Those are all the things that make a massive difference,” says Tom. “We were more worried about building a home that we wanted to live in and less worried about the resale value.” Enter arguably the standout feature of the house, which also happens to be its centrepiece, a cocooning study/library.
This was part of the second phase, which Tom says they went into with “more sober, open eyes about what it was going to cost”. The entire room is lined with bespoke joinery except for the fireplace, where a 1970s brick wall has been replaced by elegant grey gloss tiles. A corner window can swing right open and nestles in a dedicated niche. There are pocket doors between the study and the living room, which Tom says are rarely closed, but are framed by a bookshelf arch. On the living room side, the timber of the door frame is set on a slope in a subtle echo of the pyramid ceiling on the kitchen extension. Dedicated niches offer homes to various objects, artworks and books, part of the couple’s growing collection.
![tom boland home](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/14/43/tom-boland-home.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“Both Bill and I come from working-class families where there wasn’t art to pass down the generations. I find it really exciting that we’re starting to build a collection that our daughter might get one day,” says Tom. How do all these lovely things work with having a toddler in the house right now though? “She’s only been walking for about two months but things have been moving a little higher up. The living room coffee table used to have various things on it, now it’s bare,” says Tom. Now that the bulk of the renovation has been completed, Tom is adding to the couple’s collection of art and design. He sources pieces from all over the world — ceramics from Francis Gallery in Los Angeles, a painting by Sally Kindberg recently shipped over from a New York gallery, a 1970s bronze horse bought at an auction in Italy that was “quite heavy to ship”, and pieces from 8 Holland Street in London. “My husband plays violin, does meditation, all that, I just browse the internet all the time,” says Tom.
Taking their time and learning lessons as they go has had benefits beyond the budgetary, helping the couple create a more timeless, less trend-led scheme that they hope will be slower to date. “It’s funny how your design tastes change and there are a couple of finishes I would choose differently if I were doing it now, mainly the black hardware in the bathroom,” says Tom. “But on the whole I still like most things about the house. That’s why it is great not to do it all at once.”
summary: Tom Boland and his husband Billy renovated their Edwardian end-of-terrace home in north-west London in phases with architecture practice Studio McW to manage rising construction costs. Unwilling to compromise on finishes and specifications, the couple tackled the derelict kitchen first with an extension and internal courtyard to maximize light. The second phase introduced a bespoke study and library, allowing the family to create a personalized, timeless living space while collecting art and design pieces.
key_points: The couple bought the north-west London home in 2019 and lived through the first lockdown before embarking on a multi-phase renovation.
Rising construction costs and an unwillingness to compromise on finishes led the owners to tackle the project in distinct phases.
Studio McW designed a kitchen extension featuring a pyramidal-roofed side extension with an oculus and a small internal courtyard to draw in natural light.
A second phase of the renovation focused on creating a cocooning study and library lined with bespoke joinery.
Taking their time with the renovation helped the couple achieve a more timeless, less trend-led design scheme.

title: Government rejects 11th hour bid to delay Mayor's pedestrianisation of Oxford Street
author: Rachael Burford
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Oxford Street pedestrianisation to happen in September](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/03/13/10/35c1193c06ed4e0ea75e836dd6957162Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzczNDg0Mzc3-2.80677284.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) TfL sought permission to forego the full evaluation, but the local authority argued that plans to ban traffic from the capital’s flagship shopping street would lead to an increase in noise and pollution in surrounding roads. But minister’s rejected Westminster’s request on Friday. ![

Road runner: Sir Sadiq Khan is gaining highway powers over Oxford Street, ranging from pedestrianisation to potholes

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/09/18/12/48/Sadiq-Oxford-St.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Deputy council leader Tim Barnes said: "We’re extremely disappointed that MHCLG [the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government] has ignored legitimate concerns about the impact this scheme will have on central London. "Rushing pedestrianisation to meet the Mayor’s arbitrary deadline will be a disaster for local people, businesses and visitors. “The Mayor’s own submission to MHCLG showed air pollution and noise rising. We need to know how much, and how far, those problems will spread. "Important questions - on managing traffic, noise and impact on air quality all sit unanswered. "We’ve consistently said that if pedestrianisation must happen we’ll help to make it work. London deserves a world class shopping district but I’m worried we’re heading for an unmanaged mess.” He added that the council was reviewing the details of the decision and considering its next steps as work begins on the scheme. Traffic is set to be banned between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street by the end of October and a permanent design for the new layout of the road, likely to include al fresco dining areas, is set to be published by November 2027. Read More The Mayor believes pedestrianisation will boost Oxford Street’s attractiveness to shoppers, visitors and tourists and his office has previously rejected the Tory accusations that the project is being rushed. TfL has said it submitted an environmental impact assessment screening opinion to the Government in “accordance with the legal requirements”.
summary: The Government has rejected Westminster council's late bid to delay the Mayor's plan to pedestrianise Oxford Street. TfL sought to bypass a full evaluation, while the local authority argued the scheme would increase noise and pollution in surrounding areas. Traffic is scheduled to be banned between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street by the end of October.
key_points: The Government rejected Westminster council's request to delay the Oxford Street pedestrianisation scheme.
Westminster council argued the plan would increase noise and pollution in surrounding roads.
Traffic is set to be banned between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street by the end of October.
A permanent design layout, expected to include al fresco dining, will be published by November 2027.
The Mayor believes the pedestrianisation will boost the street's appeal to shoppers and tourists.

title: Chancellor Healey tears up Treasury 'rules' to push investment from London to regions
author: Tom Place; Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
!['Andy Burnham is not anti-London', says Sadiq Khan, as he praises PM's devolution plans](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/01/10/a617781fa7da5db4436dbe8b6286bbbeY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg4MzQxMjM2-2.85673244.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Schemes will in future be judged on a discount rate of 3% rather than 3.5% over periods of time, which will make it easier to demonstrate the long-term value of spending public money on building new schools and roads, among other projects.
But it will inevitably face claims that it has adopted reforms to make it easier to approve schemes which will deliver less economic value - but potentially more social benefits - outside of London.
The announcement comes ahead of a major speech on the economy Mr Healey is due to make on Monday.
![Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey (Yui Mok/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/05/09/778ee09606c63cf0bad25d040942cae8Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg4NjQ1MjA1-2.85729027.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The current rules in the Treasury “Green Book” favour London as investment in the capital tends to deliver better returns given its size and it being the country’s economic powerhouse.
Mr Healey also announced a new “place-based” business case system to channel more investment to the regions.
But Lord O’Neill of Gatley, one of Mr Burnham’s key economic advisers, has urged him to focus on London, the West Midlands and the Northern Powerhouse of Manchester, Liverpool and Leeds in his attempt to boost economic growth in Britain.
He told the Financial Times: "I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else."
Read More
He pointed to Greater Manchester as an example of economic growth and said if you could repeat that around populated areas, "then national economic performance will improve".
Mr Healey issued the warning amid the leap in Government borrowing earlier this week, reflecting concerns among lenders about the inflationary impact of the US’s war with Iran.
Mr Healey also said that he would ensure the UK emerges from his first Budget on October 28 with a solid “buffer against uncertainty”.
Economists have predicted that the fiscal buffer Rachel Reeves built up in her last budget, through a combination of tax rises and departmental spending cuts, will be squeezed by the inflationary pressures of ongoing global turmoil.
This could limit Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s ambitions to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, and spending plans across his wider agenda for Government.
summary: Chancellor John Healey is changing Treasury rules by lowering the discount rate to 3% and introducing a new place-based business case system to push public investment from London to regional areas. The reforms aim to make it easier to demonstrate the long-term value of spending on projects like schools and roads outside the capital, despite past Treasury guidelines favoring London. Meanwhile, economists predict that global pressures and government borrowing will squeeze the fiscal buffer ahead of the October 28 Budget.
key_points: Chancellor John Healey is reducing the Treasury discount rate from 3.5% to 3% to make it easier to approve regional spending projects.
A new 'place-based' business case system is being introduced to channel more investment outside of London.
Current Treasury rules in the Green Book have historically favored London because its size delivers better economic returns.
Government borrowing has increased amid concerns over the inflationary impact of the US-Iran war.
Economists warn that global turmoil and inflationary pressures will squeeze the fiscal buffer ahead of the October 28 Budget.

title: London council pays out £4,500 to autistic boy’s family after tuition delays
author: Josef Steen; Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/05/5/04/Town-Hall-9-ezgif-com-webp-to-jpg-converter.jpg?trim=0,25,0,24&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
The boy, known only as Y, received an autism diagnosis in March 2023 but had not gone to school for a “significant” amount of time. His father, Mr X, requested that Hackney Council undertake an EHC (education, health and care) needs assessment in July the following year.
Even though the council was aware at this point that Y had been out of school, it took several months to consider whether it needed to arrange alternative education for the boy – a dereliction of its legal duty under the Education Act 1996.
The law mandates that local councils should support children who are not being educated at school, such as those with special education needs and disabilities (SEND) or who have been excluded. If a child has an Education, Health and Care (EHC) Plan entitling them to funded support, local authorities have an ongoing duty to arrange the guaranteed help.
Parents or carers who ask their councils to carry out an EHC assessment for a child or young person must be told whether or not the council has agreed to assess within six weeks, and the creation of the plan itself must take no more than 20 weeks from the date it was requested. Hackney met this deadline for completing the boy’s EHC Plan, but failed to include the agreed “Education Other Than At School” (EOTAS) package until January 2025, despite Mr X requesting it earlier than November.
The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman (LGSCO) judged that during the process, which lasted several months, the council “conflated” the father’s request for EOTAS with its own duty to provide alternative education. As a result, the boy lost out on roughly a school term’s worth of teaching.
Even after the boy’s entitlement to funded tuition was agreed, he spent another half term without any teaching because the council’s £75 per hour budget had made sourcing “suitable” tutors difficult. “This is service failure by the council,” the watchdog ruled.
After Mr X later complained to the council, it missed its own Stage 1 deadline to respond by two months, for which it apologised and offered the family £200 to recognise the “time and trouble and distress and inconvenience”.
But this was far from enough for the Ombudsman, who found the council’s delays over the out-of-school education package caused the child and his family “avoidable distress”.
The watchdog recommended the council apologise and pay a total of £4,500 – £3,000 for the delay in incorporating alternative education provision into his EHC Plan, and £1,500 for the failure to deliver tuition.
Read More
A council spokesperson said: “We recognise the failings outlined in the Ombudsman’s report and are very sorry for the distress caused to the child and their family. We are implementing new systems to identify children missing school due to illness, absence, exclusion and suspension earlier, and will ensure the Ombudsman’s findings are reflected in these changes.
“This will include better engagement with schools and families to resolve issues so that children can continue to attend their current school, and a new inclusion panel to provide better oversight of children not attending school.
“In recent months we have implemented a complaints handling improvement plan including staff training and better tracking. Together, these have created additional investigation capacity and generally helped resolve complaints earlier.”
summary: Hackney Council has been ordered to pay £4,500 to the family of an autistic boy after failing to provide him with alternative education following tuition delays. The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman found that the council's delays and service failures caused avoidable distress and led to the boy missing significant schooling. The council acknowledged the failings, apologized to the family, and stated it is implementing new systems to address such issues.
key_points: Hackney Council was ordered to pay £4,500 in compensation to an autistic boy's family following educational delays.
The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman ruled that the council failed in its legal duty to arrange alternative education.
Delays and a strict £75-per-hour budget resulted in the boy losing out on months of teaching.
The council missed its own Stage 1 complaint response deadline by two months.
Hackney Council apologized for the failings and stated it is implementing new systems and a complaints handling improvement plan.

title: Three jailed for life for murdering man in north London with 'arsenal' of knives
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/05/6/21/Gregory.jpg?trim=3,0,760,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
![](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/05/6/28/FotoJet-(19).jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
Delivering his sentence, the judge said: "This was a truly wicked crime committed by very dangerous men.
"In my judgment, none of you have shown any real remorse for what you did."
He added that the violence inflicted on Mr Volquez was “grossly disproportionate to any threat he could have posed."
On walking out to the car park 30 to 40 minutes later, the men were chased and attacked by the defendants with an "arsenal of knives" and a hospital crutch.
Read More
Mr Volquez was later pronounced dead, having sustained 22 "sharp force injuries", with evidence also showing that he had been stamped on and kicked in the face by more than one person.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/05/6/03/Gregory-Catillo-Volquez.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
In a victim impact statement read out to the court, Gregory’s partner, Teresa said: “We have a daughter, a little girl, who misses her dad. She asks for him, she still expects to see him coming back. She needs his hugs, his words, and his presence.
“It is very painful to see a little girl suffering the absence of her father and how she tries to understand why he is not with us. They robbed her of the opportunity to grow up beside him, to share her birthdays, graduations and all the important moments of her life.
She added: “This tragedy not only destroyed our lives, but also broke the heart of a mother, who lost her only son. There are no words that can describe the suffering of this mother who had to say goodbye to her son in such a cruel and unjust way. Our family has been marked forever.”
Detective Inspector Jim Barry, who led the investigation, said: “Our thoughts go to Gregory’s loved ones who have demonstrated commendable togetherness and strength throughout this turbulent process.
“I know nothing will bring him home but am hopeful that this result offers justice and closure for his family, who have been left without a much-loved dad, brother, and son.
“Our team of officers showed huge tenacity to build a solid case with undisputable forensic evidence which resulted in these violent men being taken off our streets for a long, long time. It’s this hard work that is enabling the force to secure a positive outcome from 95 per cent of our murder investigations.”
summary: Three men have been sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of a man in north London following an attack with an arsenal of knives and a hospital crutch. The victim, Gregory Volquez, sustained 22 sharp force injuries and was kicked and stamped on during the assault. The judge described the crime as a truly wicked act committed by very dangerous men who showed no real remorse.
key_points: Three individuals were jailed for life for murdering Gregory Volquez in north London.
The victim was chased and attacked with an arsenal of knives and a hospital crutch.
Mr Volquez sustained 22 sharp force injuries and was stamped and kicked in the face.
The sentencing judge noted that none of the defendants showed any real remorse.

title: Plea to give Thames seals space for everyone's safety
author: Thomas Magill
content:
![Marmalade the seal on the shore of the Thames](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/d53c/live/559d9a60-a853-11f1-80f8-c33181935c5a.jpg)
Marmalade was so-called because of her golden-coloured coat
- Published
Marmalade the harbour seal was a familiar visitor to the River Thames, often popping up at Greenwich and Rotherhithe in south-east London.
She was given her nickname because of her bright golden-coloured coat.
However, as the number of seal sightings along the river increases, charity Thames Seal Watch has urged members of the public to give the animals space.
Despite looking cute, Emma Kelly from the charity says: "They can bite and they carry zoonotic diseases which are not very pleasant if you were to suffer a bite.
"They will do that to protect themselves."
She says getting close to the animals can cause them distress and stress, which could lead to their death.
![Emma Kelly, a woman with dark hair in a short bob, wearing a white shirt and glasses with a dark-coloured frame](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/51c4/live/8114a890-a854-11f1-80f8-c33181935c5a.jpg)
Emma Kelly, from Thames Seal Watch, warned members of the public that seals can bite to protect themselves
The charity says more and more of the seals are travelling further up the river, with one spotted as far west as Windsor.
It is thought there are about 3,500 seals living in the Thames and that they mostly stay around the estuary, east of London.
Marmalade was considered rare because there are only 500 harbour seals living in the river, compared with about 3,000 of the more common grey seals.
Gareth Richards from UK Seal Alliance says "seals are very transient, and will basically go to where there is good fish stocks".
He says "seals can swim from anything between 60 and 80 miles a day".
Because they are being spotted more frequently, Richards says he would like to see further protection of the animals in law.
Neither grey nor harbour seals are protected from intentional or reckless disturbance under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.
In May, UK Seal Alliance launched its Give Seals Space, external campaign, calling on the government to reconsider previous recommendations and provide the two species "with the legal protection they deserve".
The campaign warns that they are highly sensitive to disturbance from the public, animals and drones.
It states these can have long-lasting consequences to the animals' health and that it can lead to pup abandonment, wasted energy from staying alert and injuries from panic fleeing.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) says: "We have a suite of legislative protections in place which make it an offence to take, injure, capture or kill a seal."
![Members of the public throwing flowers into the River Thames in memory of Marmalade the harbour seal](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/598/cpsprodpb/89ae/live/19a6a270-a85a-11f1-ae45-e9984fc27c77.jpg)
A memorial was held for Marmalade after she died
As for Marmalade, she contracted a parasite disease and died in May.
Some volunteers from Thames Seal Watch, including Kelly, gathered at one of her favourite spots near the University of Greenwich for a short memorial.
Flowers were thrown into the river and a small plaque in her memory was erected.
Kelly says: "Marmalade was really special to the community.
"We created a community around Marmalade where there was lots of us to keep an eye on her and ensure she stayed safe."
Marmalade also helped attract a number of new volunteers to the charity, and all those at the memorial made a commitment that they would continue to help London's wildlife in the best way they can.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: Following the death of a popular golden-coated harbour seal named Marmalade, charity Thames Seal Watch has urged the public to give river seals space for everyone's safety. As seal sightings increase further up the Thames, experts warn that getting too close can cause the animals stress and lead to dangerous bites or disease transmission. Campaigners are calling for stronger legal protections against the intentional or reckless disturbance of seals.
key_points: A well-known harbour seal named Marmalade, recognizable by her golden coat, died from a parasite disease in May.
Thames Seal Watch warns that seals can bite to protect themselves and carry unpleasant zoonotic diseases.
There are an estimated 3,500 seals living in the Thames, with sightings increasing further up the river.
Neither grey nor harbour seals are currently protected from intentional or reckless disturbance under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, prompting calls for new legislation.

title: Thames Water scheme sparks row over future of popular London parkrun
author: Charlotte Lillywhite
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![The London Question: Should festivals in parks be banned?](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/11/45/0BE807FA-0F49-489C-8816-01118CC62C78.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Thames Water has planned a controversial wastewater recycling scheme in Teddington, but Kingston council has warned the proposed design changes to the project would make some of the Kingston Parkrun’s route difficult to use.
The council said disruption to Burnell Avenue Open Space and its surrounding paths would restrict physical activity and socialising.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/04/11/45/0BE807FA-0F49-489C-8816-01118CC62C78.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The proposed changes involve a longer construction period, more heavy vehicle trips, a higher number of maintenance hatches, extra access requirements and a bigger infrastructure footprint.
The council said: “It is extremely likely that Kingston Parkrun will have to stop for good. When work starts… it would be difficult for it to go ahead safely due to the construction work on the upper and lower paths.
“The green space at Burnell is important as a starting point to thin the runners out before heading onto the towpath. When the works are complete there will be 34 inspection hatches in Burnell green space which impinge on this.”
It said Kingston Parkrun sees more than 500 runners every week and is supported by up to 25 volunteers. However, Thames Water told the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) it is not correct to state Kingston Parkrun would need to stop permanently.
The spokesperson said: “Our expectation is that the event will be able to continue, although a temporary route diversion may be required during construction. We are engaging with Parkrun to explore and agree appropriate arrangements.”
Parkrun told the LDRS it makes any changes or closures subject to risk assessments and course condition requirements.
The warning came in Kingston’s response to Thames Water’s now-closed consultation on proposed design changes to the project, which it has now published.
Overall, Thames Water’s plan to ensure London has enough drinking water during times of prolonged dry weather would see up to 75 million litres of water a day taken from the Thames above Teddington Weir and transferred along a new pipeline to an existing underground tunnel.
Read More
This water would join the Lee Valley reservoirs, ready to become drinking water. It would be replaced in the Thames with “highly-treated” wastewater from Mogden Sewage Treatment Works via a new tunnel.
As part of the revised proposals, Thames Water changed the design of the proposed intake and outfall structures near Beaufort Road and Burnell Avenue – including increasing the size of the nearby control building and number of maintenance hatches needed.
It is proposing to use a bigger area to divert a power cable at a substation at Beaufort Road and to increase the number and peak levels of heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) servicing the Burnell Avenue worksite, while slashing HGV trips at the Tudor Drive worksite and removing all HGV trips from the Ham Playing Fields worksite.
Other proposed changes involve extending the construction period at the Burnell Avenue worksite and routing construction traffic through Ewell Road, on top of other roads already identified, to service the Burnell Avenue and Tudor Drive worksites.
The firm also scrapped proposals to build an intermediate shaft at Ham Playing Fields.
Kingston said that while it recognises the importance of securing long-term water supplies during drought, it has major concerns about the revised proposals and their impact on local residents, green spaces and roads.
The council said an increase in construction activity could have major traffic impacts on Burnell Avenue, Beaufort Road, Dysart Avenue and Dukes Avenue.
It raised concerns there would be more disturbance to wildlife, including badgers, and about the final quality of the wastewater being pumped into the Thames as it said the river’s chemical makeup would be changed.
The authority also said the proposals risked undermining the “perception and reality of safe recreational water use” at the River Thames’ first official bathing spot nearby, which was designated in May.
It outlined concerns about Thames Water’s handling of the consultation, as it said the council was notified late, it was not promoted enough, the response window was short and the firm did not provide inclusive opportunities for people to get involved.
Thames Water’s own consultation documents said the proposed changes mean the project would have greater impact on the area – including on recreation, health, open space, traffic, noise, air quality and a conservation area.
The scheme has attracted sustained backlash from local MPs, residents and campaigners, who have raised concerns about its potential impact on the environment, wildlife and human health. A petition demanding it is scrapped has gained more than 34,200 signatures.
A Thames Water spokesperson told the LDRS the project would keep taps flowing for millions of Londoners in times of drought, and that protecting the environment and recreational space is central to how it is developing.
The spokesperson said: “We would like to reassure river users that our proposed Teddington Direct River Abstraction project would not deteriorate water quality and would be required to meet strict environmental and water quality standards set by the Environment Agency.
“The new treated water outfall would also be located downstream of the bathing water site, and the recycled water would flow downstream over Teddington Weir into the tidal Thames, away from the designated bathing water site.
“We are continuing to work on the best ways to manage potential construction impacts, and will set out our approach in the construction traffic management plan published as part of our development consent order (DCO) application.
“We have run several rounds of public statutory and supplementary consultation, and hold regular meetings with relevant local authorities to keep them updated. Since our statutory consultation last year, we have been considering all the feedback received, engaging with stakeholders, and developing our design with information from surveys and technical assessments.”
Thames Water said it will continue to engage with locals as it prepares to apply to the Government next year for a development consent order to build the project.
Ali McArthur, global head of event delivery and volunteering at Parkrun, said: “The majority of parkrun events take place on public land, and we have robust safety and policy procedures in place to ensure people can walk, jog, run, or volunteer safely.
“We appreciate the land use granted to us by all the landowners we work with, and any course adjustments or closures happen subject to risk assessments and course condition requirements. We always work closely with landowners and event teams to try and keep communities connected and active wherever possible.”
summary: Thames Water's proposed wastewater recycling scheme in Teddington has sparked concern from Kingston council, which warns that design changes could force the Kingston Parkrun to stop permanently. The council cited issues including a longer construction period, increased heavy vehicle traffic, and numerous inspection hatches that would disrupt the event's route at Burnell Avenue Open Space. However, Thames Water stated it expects the event to continue with potential temporary diversions, and is engaging with Parkrun to explore arrangements.
key_points: Kingston council warned that Thames Water's revised scheme could force the Kingston Parkrun to stop permanently due to construction impacts on paths and green space.
Thames Water stated it is not correct that the Parkrun must stop permanently and expects the event to continue with possible temporary route diversions.
The controversial wastewater recycling scheme aims to secure drinking water during dry weather by taking water from the Thames and replacing it with treated wastewater.
The council also raised concerns over increased traffic, construction duration, wildlife disturbance, and potential impacts on a nearby official river bathing spot.

title: Dedicated officer to combat homes pumping sewage into waterways
author: Luxmy Gopal
content:
![Man in a pink hi-viz coat and rubber gloves holding a jar of murky water while he stares at it in a concerned manner.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/20ca/live/500d4200-a6df-11f1-9e4c-79c1c0e340c6.jpg)
Volunteer Ben Morris said he welcomed tougher action on sewage leaked from housing
- Published
A dedicated officer is to be hired in west London in a trial to combat the problem of water-polluting misconnections.
Owing to incorrect plumbing, affected households pump waste into surface drains, which can then spread, killing wildlife and damaging waterways.
Local authorities can take enforcement action, and if the pilot - funded by the mayor of London's office - is successful, the measure could be rolled out across the capital.
Funding is to be spent where the issue is considered a particular problem, including the River Brent catchment area.
Founder of the volunteer group Clean Up the River Brent (CURB), Ben Morris, said there was "good reason" to think misconnections "are the biggest single cause of pollution in London's rivers".
He added: "We need to see stronger action from the councils to get this done.
"They have the power of enforcement and they need to be using those powers to get those property owners to sort out the misconnections."
![Deputy mayor Mete Coban standing in front of a hedge, wearing a white T-shirt and black cardigan.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/e197/live/26299320-a6e0-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Deputy mayor Mete Coban says the trial could be expanded across London
An information request to Thames Water by the charity Friends of the River Crane Environment (FORCE ) revealed that in October 2024 seven blocks of flats in north and west London were identified as having misconnections.
FORCE said this meant at least 100 homes were flushing waste into the rivers Crane and Brent.
Since then, only three of the seven blocks' misconnections have been resolved, according to Thames Water.
The company said two of the housing developments still pumping out sewage were in the borough of Barnet, while two were in the borough of Harrow.
It said the other three, which were in Ealing borough, have since had their misconnections fixed.
It did not provide details of where exactly the properties are.
Barnet Council said it was committed to resolving misconnections "as quickly and effectively as possible".
Harrow Council's press office did not respond to the BBC's request for a response.
![Close-up of a gloved hand checking a strip of paper against a chart to see what chemicals are present in water. There is an out-of-focus stream in the background and some plants at the water's edge.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/0828/live/084bda70-a6e0-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
The volunteer group CURB measures pollution levels in the River Brent
Mete Coban, deputy mayor of London for environment, said the project would "beef up" councils by giving them resources needed to properly enforce action against misconnections.
"City Hall has funded a dedicated officer to operate within the council, to get to the root cause of misconnections, working with the landlords and others to make sure that we're actually dealing with this issue."
The project is part of a 10-year plan to clean up some of London's rivers and waterways, announced by Sir Sadiq Khan in July.
Among ten locations earmarked for funding are the Grand Union Canal, the River Brent catchment area, and the Lower Crane Valley.
A total of Â£1.8bn has been pledged by water companies, boroughs and charities, with London's mayor adding Â£2.7m across three years, on top of Â£13.6m already promised.
![Man in a pink hi-viz jacket puts a stick into a murky stream](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/da82/live/c2c03ea0-a6e0-11f1-acae-21b536d72e0e.jpg)
Ben Morris sets up sewage monitoring devices in west London waterways
A Thames Water spokesperson said households and buildings which have connected wastewater appliances to the wrong drainage system can have a serious impact on the environment.
"While we are not responsible for third-party drainage, we work closely with partners to tackle this significant issue across our catchment. Of the seven cases identified across North and West London, three have now been resolved, while work continues on the remaining cases.
"Most misconnections are done entirely by accident, but the responsibility remains with the property owner, which is why we would urge freeholders or developers fitting new connections to make sure they're plumbed in properly."
A Barnet Council spokesperson said the investigations "can be complex, involving multiple people and organisations" but they were "committed to resolving them as quickly and effectively as possible".
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: A trial funded by the mayor of London's office will hire a dedicated officer in west London to combat water-polluting household misconnections that pump sewage into surface drains. Incorrect plumbing causes wastewater to damage waterways and kill wildlife, making enforcement action essential. If successful, the pilot measure could be expanded across the capital as part of a broader 10-year plan to clean up London's rivers.
key_points: A dedicated officer is being hired in west London in a trial to tackle sewage-polluting household misconnections.
Incorrect plumbing causes homes to pump waste into surface drains, which harms waterways and wildlife.
An information request revealed that at least 100 homes across seven blocks of flats in north and west London were flushing waste into local rivers, with four blocks remaining unresolved.
The pilot project is funded by the mayor of London's office and is part of a 10-year plan to clean up London waterways.

title: 'Game of Thrones: The Mad King' to transfer to London in 2027 | London Theatre
author: Olivia Rook
content:
![](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/49MI1aQ1PfZh0FBi2kRMWF/7b5c54f563fe7a1b2d02667f60cdd93b/Game_of_Thrones_1200_LT_George_R._R._Martin_London_Announcement_Image.jpg?h=200&fm=webp&q=90)
![](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/49MI1aQ1PfZh0FBi2kRMWF/7b5c54f563fe7a1b2d02667f60cdd93b/Game_of_Thrones_1200_LT_George_R._R._Martin_London_Announcement_Image.jpg?h=550&fm=webp&q=90)
'Game of Thrones: The Mad King' to transfer to London in 2027
Based on novels by George R. R. Martin, and adapted by Duncan Macmillan and directed by Dominic Cooke, The Mad King is a prequel to the acclaimed TV series about noble houses fighting for control of the Iron Throne.
![Olivia Rook](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/2AnVizCwXsbKHoScEZBHKl/7b2e062e88ede030d9eea0db2bb6a632/Author_bio_pic_for_website.jpg?w=32&h=32)
The Royal Shakespeare Company production of George R. R. Martin’s new play Game of Thrones: The Mad King will open in London in 2027.
Based on novels by George R. R. Martin, and adapted by Duncan Macmillan and directed by Dominic Cooke, The Mad King is a prequel to the acclaimed TV series about noble houses fighting for control of the Iron Throne.
The play received its world premiere at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon in August, and finishes its run tomorrow (5 September).
Creator and Executive Producer George R. R. Martin said: “I had an absolutely splendid time in Stratford upon Avon for the premier and am thrilled the production will be moving to London to share the experience with a wider audience. It promises to be an exhilarating journey.”
The RSC production's creative team includes puppetry and movement directors Nick Barnes and Finn Caldwell (Lume), set designer Chloe Lamford, costume designer Georgia McGuinness, lighting designer Jon Clark, composer Will Stuart, sound designer Tom Gibbons, fight director Bethan Clark, intimacy director Ingrid Mackinnon, voice and text coach Jeannette Nelson, and dialect coach Hazel Holder.
Venue, dates, and casting will be announced in due course.
